Indeed, up to the present day, many Sanskrit works have been edited by eminent scholars here and there in this land of Bhārata and brought to light through the medium of printing.
Nevertheless, certain ancient compositions, though worthy of publication, remain hidden within the very depths of manuscript libraries.
Among those, this work titled *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha* is now being published with great effort for the delight of the hearts of connoisseurs.
The author of this treatise, the *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha*, is Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa;
[he is also known as] Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa or Ācārya Udbhaṭa.
The mention of Jayāpīḍa by this name is seen in other texts;
from Kalhaṇa’s excellent *Rājatarangiṇī*, it is understood that Udbhaṭabhaṭṭa was the court poet (*sabhāpati*) of King Jayāpīḍa in Kashmir.
It is known that the period of King Jayāpīḍa’s reign lasted from the year 779 CE until 813 CE.
Therefore, it is the conclusion of scholars that the period of Udbhaṭabhaṭṭa, the president of that assembly, was also that very same time.
It is known that Ācārya Udbhaṭa composed the poem titled *Kumārasambhava* as well as a commentary on the work on poetics (*alaṅkāra*) written by Bhāmaha.
The evidence for this is found in this *Laghuvṛtti*: "By this author [Udbhaṭa], a portion of his own composed *Kumārasambhava*..."

The statement of Pratihārendurāja is as follows: "On page 15, [the example] is presented here as an illustration; and on page 13, in his commentary on Bhāmaha’s *Viśeṣokti*, Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa explained the term ‘ekadeśavivarti’ in this very manner. Furthermore, the author of the *Kāvyālaṅkārasāralaghuvṛtti*, the illustrious Pratihārendurāja, was a resident of the Koṅkaṇa country who [later] resided in Kaśmīra.
That he studied the scriptures under the venerable Bhaṭṭa Mukula, who was a master of the treatises on Mīmāṃsā, grammar, logic,
and literature, is made clear by the two verses found at the beginning and conclusion of this *Laghuvṛtti*:
"Having learned [it] from Mukulaka, the foremost among the wise, it is now being explained..."
The *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha* was composed by Pratihārendurāja, who is a moon over the ocean of words born from the cloud that is the essence of Mīmāṃsā; a casket of rubies of logic;
the splendor of poetry belonging to Murāri; a bee at the lotus-feet of Śauri; and a flower for the wise.
Having heard [this] from the bud-like mouth of the best of the twice-born— a reservoir of benevolence and a basin for the creeper of fame—
Śrī Indurāja of Koṅkaṇa composed this short commentary on the *Kāvyālaṅkārasāra*. Thus,
it is impossible to determine with certainty the time of Pratihārendurāja’s life.
Nevertheless, it is quite clear that this [author] lived after Udbhaṭa;

for in his *Laghuvṛtti*, he mentions only ancient rhetoricians such as Bhāmaha, Vāmana, and Udbhaṭa, but not later rhetoricians such as Mahimabhaṭṭa, Ānandavardhana, or the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Therefore, it is inferred that he lived between the ninth and tenth centuries of the Christian era.

the first chapter,
accompanied by the *Kāvyālaṅkārasāralaghuvṛtti* composed by the illustrious Pratīhārendurāja.
That which was whitened here by the white smiles of Lakṣmī as she indulged in playful jests with Śauri;
that which was reddish-pink in some places by the radiance of the expansive rays of the Kaustubha gem;
and elsewhere, which was streaked by the spreading splendor of golden light.
May that chest of his, resembling the sky variegated by an unblemished rainbow, protect the world. // 1 //

O Gaurī, I bow to your pair of feet, which grant fearlessness to the inhabitants of heaven when they were shown terror by the enemy of the gods who had assumed the body of a buffalo, and which are worshipped by the joyful Lord of the Suras. // 2 //
Having acquired [this work] from Mukulaka, the foremost among the learned, Pratīhārendurāja now explains the *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha*. (3)
The semblance of tautology (punaruktavadābhāsa) and alliteration (anuprāsa)—
which is of three kinds, including the Lāṭānuprāsa— and metaphor (rūpaka), which is of four kinds, constitute the figures of speech.
"Simile, as well as Illuminator (dīpaka) and the Simile by Correspondence (prativastūpamā)—these alone are the ornaments of speech cited by some. (UK 1.2)

Eight ornaments have been indicated here; among them, first, four verbal ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra) have been described. However, the four beginning with metaphor (rūpaka) constitute verbal ornaments in this context. As for the other four, they are ornaments of meaning (arthālaṅkāra).
In this context, the mention of "threefold" for alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and "fourfold" for metaphor (*rūpaka*) is intended to dispel misconceptions.
For Bhāmaha explained alliteration as having only two varieties—vulgar (*grāmya*) and refined (*upanāgaraka*)—according to the distinction of poetic meters (*vṛtta*).
Likewise, regarding metaphor, he demonstrated only the first two of the four varieties that will be described hereafter.

Therefore, by way of demonstrating the divisions favored by [the author] himself, in order to dispel such misconceptions, it was stated at the very stage of the enumeration (uddeśa) that "alliteration is threefold" and "metaphor (rūpaka) is fourfold. In the phrase "metaphor is fourfold," existence (sattā), which resides in a single object together with the nature of metaphor, is perceived as recurring within the various instances of metaphor.

Therefore, regarding that very act of becoming (*bhavanakriyā*), which is perceived as being inherent in the single entity that is the metaphor (*rūpaka*) and whose essence is existence (*sattā*), this suffix *suc* is applied according to the rule "after the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the suffix] *suc*" (Pāṇini 5.4.18).
The meaning is that the metaphor exists four times by way of its fourfold divisions.
In this regard, that which appears as a tautology (punaruktavadābhāsa) is explained as follows:

"A word with a distinct form that appears as if its meaning were non-distinct is 'appearing as a tautology' (punaruktābhāsa). That in which a non-distinct object (*abhinnavastu*) shines forth is 'a non-distinct object'."
The two words whose forms are distinct are "distinct-form" (*bhinnarūpe*).

That in which two distinct-form words shine forth constantly as if they were a single, non-distinct entity is "a distinct-form word shining forth as if it were a non-distinct entity" (*abhinnavastvivodbhāsi-bhinnarūpapada*).
Thus, this is a five-word *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it two [embedded] *bahuvrīhi*s.
In this regard, one [term] is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "having an undivided object," while the other is "having a divided form.
And this *bahuvrīhi* contains within it a word that appears as having an undivided object, even though its form is divided.

And by this [definition], that poetic ornament which is to be embellished— wherein two words of different forms appear as if they possessed a single meaning— is designated as *punaruktābhāsa* (the semblance of tautology).

Although the suffix *-vat* was employed in the formal statement (*uddeśa*) as "resembling a tautology" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsam*), it is nevertheless not used here because its meaning is already understood.
However, this omission in the summary is for the purpose of demonstrating the variety of expression;
for indeed, some expression proceeds by way of the connection with a meaning that is already implied.
However, in some cases, the expression is shown through the connection with the similarity of the meaning being explicitly stated;
there, in the *uddeśa*, the expression is demonstrated through the connection with the similarity of what is explicitly stated by the suffix *-vat*;
here, however, it is through the connection with the similarity that is to be understood by the force of the context (*arthasāmarthya*).
Thus, in this manner, the poetic figure *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the appearance of repetition) is here the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) of the poem (*kāvyam*), which is the object to be adorned (*alaṅkāryam*).

It has been stated that the status of being an ornament belongs to the two words that appear as if repeated, because they possess the quality of being a poem; it is not [an ornament] in its own right.
And the purpose of expressing it in this way is to demonstrate that the connection of words appearing as if repeated constitutes a poetic figure.
Indeed, when the nature of an ornament is defined through its dependence upon that which is to be adorned, its true essence is properly defined;
for as long as it remains in itself, it is not an ornament,
just like necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments when they are kept inside a casket.

Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to describe this as a semblance of tautology (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*) in order to demonstrate its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), since it is dependent upon the poetic context.
An example of this is as follows:
"From that time forth, he remained free from attachment, wearing the skin of the elephant-king..."
Śitikaṇṭha suffered the agony of the fire of grief for Satī, who had perished at the time of her death.
From that time forward—that is, beginning from the separation from Satī—that blue-throated god, being detached, passed his days; this completes the sense of the sentence in the verse to be cited.
*Kṛtti* means skin.
[The phrase] "returning by the power of time" refers to that which...
He is so described because he possesses the suffering arising from that fire of grief produced by separation from Satī.
Here, the words *nāgakuñjara* and *śitikaṇṭha-kālagala* appear as if they were redundant.
For instance, when the words *nāga* and *kuñjara* are uttered together, they appear to have a single meaning by virtue of both denoting an elephant;
however, this is sublated upon careful reflection on the connection between the word-meanings.
In this context, the word *nāga* indeed denotes an elephant;
the word *kuñjara*, however, is understood as a term of praise for it.
The same applies to the pair of words *śitikaṇṭha* and *kālagala*.

The possibility of tautology—which might arise from the expression of distinct meanings belonging to different parts of the body demarcated by specific folds—is set aside as it vanishes with time; furthermore, this is removed by considering the limit at the letter *ta*.
Therefore, in this case, there is the figure of speech known as "semblance of tautology" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*).
Now, one might object: "Is not the example of 'semblance of tautology' recited immediately after the definition of 'alliteration' (*chekānuprāsa*)?"
But why was its presentation made at this very moment, during the explanation of the definition of what "appears as a repetition"?
It is said in reply:
there is no fault here, for it was presented right now because the meaning of the definition is difficult to comprehend without the demonstration of an example.

Likewise, in what follows as well, one should not be critical when the commentary explains by following the sequence of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), even if this results in a reversal of the order of the text's recitation;
for the sequence of meaning is more powerful than the sequence of recitation.
[This concludes the section on] *chekānuprāsa*.
Chekānuprāsa, however, consists in the production of very similar sounds between pairs [of syllables].
When the utterance of two successive groups of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*) is performed such that they are very similar to one another, *chekānuprāsa* occurs.
Such groups attain the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāratā*) therein.

Regarding the expression "of each pair" (*dvayordvayoḥ*), since the repetition (*dvirvacana*) is used in its own sense (*svārtha*)—as the inclusion of the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is excluded by the use of the word "own"—it does not refer to all possible pairs that may exist here.
The state of being very similar must apply to all of them; why then [is it said] "of only some"?
For repetition occurs when there is totality.
And that [resemblance] has been rejected here by the term "for its own sake" (svārtha).
Furthermore, because of the mention of "being determined," it should be understood that the similarity here exists only between each pair of groups,
and not between all three together.
And because of the expression "in many [instances]," it should be understood that *chekānuprāsa* occurs only when such a form is employed repeatedly, and not merely once.

Letters or groups of letters that are mutually endowed with a single form, which have attained excellence by being conducive to the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, and which are introduced into poetry as a cause for an extraordinary beauty, are designated by the term *anuprāsa*, which has a corresponding etymological meaning.
By the word *cheka*, birds that delight in their nests are designated.
As it has been said: “The beasts and birds envy the *chekas* for their dwelling in their homes.
And because they delight in their nests and are not disturbed by anyone else, a sweet voice similar to this alliteration issues forth from them.

Therefore, this alliteration is designated by the learned as *c hekānuprāsa* (the alliteration of the clever). Alternatively, *c hekāḥ* refers to the refined; it is called *c hekānuprāsa* because it is beloved by them.
An illustration of this is as follows:
"That god spent his days in that cave of the lord of mountains, attended by the Pramathas, who were the foremost in the most distinguished assemblies."
*Kandara* means a cave.
*Gariṣṭhāḥ* means the heaviest;
here, by the rule of the superlative suffix *-iṣṭhan*, the word *guru* undergoes the substitution of *gara*.
A gathering of the learned is the formal seating of the foremost and preeminent Pramathas,
the divine hosts.
"Paryupāsitaḥ" means "served" or "attended.

Here, the pairs of vowel-consonant clusters (*ajjhalsamudāya*)—namely *sadeva-divasa* and *indrakandara*, *gariṣṭha-goṣṭhī* and *prathamapramatha*, and *paryupāsa* and *paryupāsa*—are recited with great similarity; therefore, there is *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration).
In some places, however, where the reading is "tasmin ninye," there is a variant reading "anyasmin ninye.
In that case, this too is included among the examples [of alliteration].
This is *anuprāsa* (alliteration).
And that [style] is threefold, depending on the modes of expression (vṛtti),
as he will say:
"The arrangement of similar vowels and consonants occurs in these three modes of expression."
"Poets always desire alliteration (anuprāsa) to be distinct and separate.
The meaning of this is as follows:

among these three types of phonetic arrangements—which, as appropriate, are conducive to the manifestation of rasa and other aesthetic qualities—poets always desire that alliteration consist of the arrangement of similar consonants (vyañjana) in a manner that is distinct and separate.
Therefore, those *vṛttis* (styles), which consist of the employment of phonemes conducive to the manifestation of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth, are described first.
And they are threefold, distinguished as *paruṣā* (harsh), *upanāgarikā* (polished), and *grāmyā* (vulgar).
Among those, the harsh (paruṣā) style is that which is joined with the letters śa and ṣa, with clusters containing the letter ra,
with the *iṣṭa* group of consonants, and with combinations such as *hl*, *hv*, and *hy*.
The usage of phonemes joined with *ś*, *ṣ*, and so forth is the mode of expression known as "harsh" (*paruṣā*).
Consonant clusters characterized by the letter *r*, such as *kr* and others, are "repha-conjunctions.
The group of consonants characterized by the letter *ṭ* is the "ṭa-group," namely *ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa*.
The alliteration (*anuprāsa*) found in this *vṛtti* is the harsh alliteration (*paruṣānuprāsa*).
An example of it is as follows:
"There, the lotuses (*kuśeśaya*), which had been entirely unfolded by the hope for water..."
Autumn shone forth, its quarters at the horizon tawny with the ripened stalks of rice and *kiṃśuka* flowers.
The compound [toyaśayeṣu] means that by which lotuses (*kuśeśaya*)—that is, water-lilies (*padma*)—have been entirely and completely blossomed or opened within the reservoirs of water.

Likewise, the compound [āśāmukha] means that the faces of the quarters—the openings of the directions—in which are brownish-yellow (*kapiśa*), that is, tawny, due to the awns (*kiṃśāru*) or spikes of the *śāli* rice grains.
Furthermore, this constitutes a harsh alliteration (*paruṣānuprāsa*) because of the arrangement of the letter *śa* based on its similarity.
The Upanāgarikā style—

scholars consider that [rhetorical figure] to be Upanāgarikā which consists of similar syllables joined by conjuncts, and which is joined with the final consonants of the vargas at the head [of the word]. (UK 1.5)
The *upanāgarikā* style consists of consonants joined with combinations of similar-sounding letters (*sarūpa-varṇa*), such as *kk*, *pp*, *cc*, and so forth;

likewise, it consists of the stops (*sparśa*) from *k* to *m* joined above with the final letters of the classes (*vargāntya*)—namely *ṅ*, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *m*—in forms such as *ṅka*, *ñca*, *ṇṭa*, *nta*, and *mpa*.
This style is indeed compared to a refined (*nāgarikā*) woman who possesses cleverness (*vaidagdhī*); therefore, it is called *upanāgarikā*.
It is called *upanāgarikā* because it is compared (*upamitā*) to a city-dweller (*nāgarikā*).
The compound is formed according to the rule: "Verbs such as *ava* [and others] are compounded with an instrumental case when they have the sense of 'reaching' (*ṛṣṭa*, etc.).
Alliteration belonging to that [style] is *upanāgarikānuprāsa*.
And an example of that is as follows: In one place, [the forest] gladdened the bees with a beautiful movement, through trickling drops of honey-water arising from dense clusters of lotuses.
Here, the contact consonant known as *da* is joined with the letter *na* situated above it, being thus composed according to their formal similarity (*sārūpya*).
The connection is: "the thick, dense drops of nectar-water arising from the clusters of lotuses.

In the phrase "with those that possess beautiful vibration" (*sundaraspandibhiḥ*), the general term "vibration" (*spanda*) is qualified by the specific vibration "beautiful vibration," just as in the expression "it nourishes the nourishment of beauty" (*raipoṣaṃ puṣṇāti*).

In the compound *sundara-spandaḥ*, where "that in which there is beautiful vibration" is the general sense of the whole, the word "vibration" (*spandana*)— qualified by "beauty"— constitutes the meaning of the subordinate member (*vṛtti-pada*). *Indindiras* are bees.

Those whose intellects are honored [by the wise] praise the *grāmyā* (rustic) style— which is described by the remaining phonemes as appropriate under the name "soft" (*komala*)— as the mode of expression (*vṛtti*) in poetic compositions.
That which is composed of letters beginning with *la* and the like—remaining after the letters employed in the *paruṣā* (harsh) and *upanāgarikā* (slightly refined) styles—is the *grāmyā* (vulgar).
Furthermore, another name for that very same [style] is *komalā* (tender);
the connection is that it is described by the name *komalā*.
And in that [type of alliteration], there is vulgar alliteration (*grāmyānuprāsa*).
An example of it is as follows:
"In some places, by the sweet, tumultuous sounds of swarms of bees restless with play..."
It produced the illusion of the sound of anklets belonging to the Goddess of Fortune as she ascended the forest.
"Addicted to play" means those who are devoted to sporting. "With sweet tones" means with melodious sounds.
"Delusion" refers to error, which is a cognition of inversion.
Here, the letters *la*, *ka*, *ra*, and *repha* are arranged according to their similarity.
Thus, these three types of *vṛtti* have been explained.
And within them, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is employed individually in accordance with the manifestation of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth; as it has been said:

Poets always desire the *anuprāsa* (alliteration) to be distinct in each of these three modes of operation, provided that the phonemes (*vyañjana*) and their forms (*sarūpa*) are arranged accordingly.
This verse, along with its illustration, has been explained in the context of defining the nature of *vṛtti*.
As for *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the Lāṭas):
"Even when there is no difference in form or meaning, repetition [occurs] for the sake of another purpose."
The *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) is desired in the case of either words (*śabda*) or phrases (*pada*).
By virtue of abiding in two words, one of the two is as before;
because the other is independent, or because both depend on a single word.
Through the application of two [lines] either as independent phrases or as a single unit,
it is divided in many ways by various distinctions and by means of the sequence of repeating the lines.
Even when there is no difference— whether among words whose *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are not perceived, or words whose *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes are perceived,

or among both types of words and phrases— with respect to their own nature consisting of phonemes, as well as their denoted meaning which is the object of continuous verbal activity, repetition occurs due to a difference in intention (*tātparya*) arising from a different result; because it is favored by the inhabitants of the Lāṭa country, it is called *lāṭānuprāsa*.
And that [non-existence] is first of all threefold,
because there is non-existence in two independent [entities], in two dependent [entities], and in both independent and dependent [entities].
Among these, that which pertains to two independent [entities] is twofold.
Because it exists in each individual word as well as in the verse consisting of a collection of words,
it has been said:
"Whether by means of independent word-forms or through the employment of two [words together]..."
It is divided into many varieties through various distinctions and by means of the sequence of repeated feet.
"Thus;
for here, because both [types] consist of independent words, the *lāṭānuprāsa* based on individual words has been described through their combined application.
An example of it is as follows:"
The *kāśa* flowers shimmered like *kāśa* flowers, and the lakes were like lakes;
they stirred the hearts of the youths as rivers stir other rivers.
They explained, that is, they taught:
here, words such as *kāśa* and others are identical in form and identical in referent with other words such as *kāśa* and others;
however, their repetition occurs due to a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*).
For in this case, some words such as *kāśa* and others are employed with reference to substances qualified by a distinction of genus (*jāti*),
while others are employed with reference to the exclusion of other points of comparison through the shadow of the figure of speech known as *ananvaya*.
And here, the words possess independence (*svātantrya*).
Because words such as *kāśa* and others are perceived in the form of nominal stems (*su*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*),
their arrangement occurs through repetition in their individual forms.

However, when a verse-quarter (*pāda*) consisting of a collection of words is repeated— while its essential nature and meaning remain unchanged but with a difference in intended emphasis (*tātparya*)— it constitutes *lāṭānuprāsa*, which relies on independent words through the sequence of repeating verse-quarters.

By the inclusion of the term "successively" (*krama*) in the phrase "by means of the successive repetition of quarters" (*pādābhyāsakrameṇa*), the application of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration in the sense of regional usage) is indicated as occurring when the various varieties possible through the repetition of a quarter once, twice, or thrice are accepted.
An example of this is:
"Women did not become angry with their husbands even when a great offense was committed."
Even their husbands did not become angry with the women, even when they had committed an offense.
The connection is with the phrase "even though the offense is great.
Thus, even when an offense exists, the status of being a *saṃpradāna* (recipient) according to the rule "in relation to *krudh*, *druh*, etc. applies to both "toward husbands" and "toward women.
Here, in one quarter of the verse, the absence of anger on the part of the woman is established with respect to the offense committed by the hero.

In another instance, however, what is described is the absence of anger on the part of the hero directed toward an offense committed by the heroine consisting of her transgression against the husband's affection;

thus, while there is a difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is no difference in the essential nature of the meaning (*svarūpārtha*). Furthermore, there is the repetition of a *pāda*, which consists of a collection of words.
Thus, this *lāṭānuprāsa* based on independent words has been described as being of two kinds:
that which rests on individual words and that which rests on a collection of words.
Furthermore, there are also two types of *lāṭānuprāsa* involving two dependent words for which neither the nominal (*su*) nor the verbal (*tiṅ*) endings are perceived.
By virtue of being the locus for two words and having a single word as its support;
as it has been said:
"It [the *vṛtti*] exists in both by means of abiding in two words."
The connection is that "it is divided in many ways by means of divisions. Likewise, [there is division] "from the basis of two or one word.
An example of the former is as follows:
In some places there were blossoming lotuses with bees hovering over them,
and there were noisy cranes and the warbling of bees.
*Sārasas* are a specific kind of bird known by the name *lakṣmaṇa*.

Here, although there is a difference in the literal form and meaning of the words "lotus" (*kamala*) and "bee" (*ṣaṭpada*), there is a repetition [of the same idea] due to a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), as well as a reliance on two distinct words.
And the difference in intended meaning here arises from the difference in the functional capacities (*kāraka-śakti*) of the words "lotus" and "bee."
For instance:

the first word "kamala" (lotus) is employed here with reference to its being the agent of the action of blooming, whereas the latter is [employed] as the locus for the bee that is the agent of the action of wandering.
Likewise, the first word "ṣaṭpada" is described as the agent with respect to the action of wandering,
whereas the latter is connected to the action of buzzing; however, the two words "mukhara" [function differently].
The quality of being accompanied by the word "with" (sa-śabdatva), functioning as a qualifier, causes one to understand [the object] as residing in a distinct referent;
for instance:
By the word *mukhara* in the first instance, talkativeness residing in the autumn season is understood;
by the other [instance], however, it refers to that residing in the cranes (*sārasa*).
Thus, this *lāṭānuprāsa*, which relies on two words dependent upon two distinct words, has been described.
However, that which resides in two words based on a single word-base is described by the rule: "Or [the compound occurs] because of being based on a single word-base for two [words].
An example of this is:
*jitānyapuṣṭakiñjalkakiñjalkaśreṇiśobhitam* (adorned with rows of filaments as yellow as the filaments of other flowers).
The blue lotus became an ear-ornament upon the moon-like faces of women.
Here, by stating "in the faces of women," since the faces are compared to the moon, the black lotus is suggested (dhvanita) to be of the nature of the hare-mark [on the moon].

Furthermore, in this case, the words *kiñjalka* and *śaśaka* share an identity in their literal meaning (*svarūpārtha*) and reside in a single word-form, yet there is a difference in their intended meaning (*tātparyabheda*),
because one is employed as that which is being surpassed.
This series [of sounds] belongs to the other [word], which has become the agent of the action of conquering;
thus, this *lāṭānuprāsa* of two dependent words has been described as being of two kinds.
However, in the case of independent and dependent words, where one word enters into another word—
But for the other, there occurs an independent existence in the form of a word (*pada*).
As it has been said: "Of one [the state is] as before; of the other, because of its independence.
The meaning is that for the one, it exists by depending on another word, as was the case previously.

An illustration of this is as follows: Having come from Lake Mānasa, the abode of the swan-folk, the swans— driven by an intense longing for lotus ponds— made the [other] lotus ponds appear uneven within [by their own presence].
"From the Mānasa, a particular lake.
They made [the swans] appear as if they had protruding tusks because of their great size and whiteness.

Here, although there is no difference in the literal meaning of the two words *padminī* and the two words *haṃsa*, there is no tautology because of the difference in their intended significance (*tātparya*).
For one [word] there is the entry into another word,
and for the other, it is for the purpose of conveying the object of desire;
likewise, because one *haṃsa* word denotes the meaning of the agent of the action of "teeth-baring."
But for another [type], it is due to its connection with a word-group (kula).
Thus, this fivefold *lāṭānuprāsa* has been explained;

for among those that are independent (*svatantra*) and dependent (*paratantra*), there are two varieties for each, and because the independent and dependent [types] taken together constitute a single variety.
Metaphor (rūpaka)—
when, due to the absence of a connection through direct hearing (śruti), one word is joined with another primary word by means of a secondary function (guṇavṛtti), that is indeed metaphor. (UK 1.11)
Because its definition is established by both the literal word and the intended meaning of the scripture,
it [the *upamāna*] has as its object either the entirety of things or only a single part thereof.

Metaphor in the form of a garland (*mālārūpaka*) is said to have all things as its object, or it may occur with respect to a single part, because of the representation [of one thing] through the form of another. (UK 1.13)
When a word functioning through a secondary figurative sense (guṇavṛtti) is joined with another word, a metaphor (rūpaka) arises.

Anticipating the objection that "if this were so, then even in the case of 'a blue lotus' (nīlam utpalam), the word 'blue'—functioning figuratively as a quality—would result in a metaphor when joined with the word 'lotus'," it is stated: "because of the absence of a connection by direct denotation" (śrutyā saṃbandhavirahāt).
Here, "direct denotation" (śruti) refers to the operation of a word directed toward its primary, immediate meaning.

When, through that [primary] sense, another word whose connection with other words is otherwise untenable is applied figuratively (guṇavṛtti) so as to be joined with another word, there is metaphorical identification (rūpaka).
For example:
"The sky, variegated with star-flowers, is sprinkled by the water of moonlight from the jar of the moon."
Gradually, the garden of the sky was sprinkled by the maidens of the night.
Thus,

in this case, the word *ambu* (water), which refers to the generic property of waterness (*udakatva*) as brought within the scope of the operation of a word denoting an uninterrupted object, does not experience grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *jyotsnā* (moonlight).
This is because there is no inherence (*samavāya*) of the two properties— waterness and moonlightness— in a single substratum.

Therefore, because the word *ambu* possesses qualities—such as being watery, white, refreshing, and flowing—that are similar to the qualities residing in moonlight (*jyotsnā*), it functions through metaphorical application (*guṇavṛtti*) toward the moonlight.

Consequently, since the word *ambu* lacks a connection with the other word *jyotsnā* through its primary denotative function (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) which, by virtue of direct hearing (*śruti*), is fixed upon an uninterrupted object, it is a case of metaphorical usage.
Thus, in this instance:

In cases such as "a blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), there is no metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*) because the relationship [between the qualities] is absent through direct denotation (*śruti*); rather, it occurs by its own nature (*svata eva*). Thus, there is no undesirable consequence of it being a metaphor (*rūpakatā*).

Now, if two words in grammatical apposition that express contradictory meanings— because their denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), which rests upon their immediate referents, cannot establish a mutual connection between them— must have one of them function through indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
then it follows that here there would be a turn-taking (*paryāya*) in the application of secondary figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*),
since there is no rule to determine otherwise.

Furthermore, just as it was stated that the word *ambu* functions figuratively (*guṇavṛtti*) because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *jyotsnā*, one might raise the objection: "Why should the word *jyotsnā* not likewise function figuratively because of its coreferentiality with the word *ambu*? Anticipating this, it is said: "By the primary [term]. It is logical that the subordinate term functions figuratively through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in accordance with the meaning of the primary term.
The intention is that qualities (guṇas) are subject to the influence of the primary element (pradhāna).

Therefore, because the word *jyotsnā* (moonlight) expresses the contextual meaning and thus pertains to the primary object, it is logical—by following that word—that the word *ambu* (water), which does not express the contextual meaning and thus pertains to a non-primary object, functions as a quality (*guṇavṛtti*); hence, it is not a mere synonym (*paryāya*).
There would be the undesirable consequence of both "moonlight" (*jyotsnā*) and "water" (*ambu*) functioning as subordinate qualities (*guṇavṛtti*) through mutual dependence.
But is it not the case that in the expression *jyotsnāmbunā*, water is the primary element and moonlight is subordinate?
For it is thus:

In this verse, through the determination of that state (*tadbhāvādhyavasānena*), the pervasion of the sky—which was explained as "it was sprinkled" (*asicyata*) by virtue of its form being veiled by the sprinkling and thus having the nature of the sprinkling—is here qualified by moonlight; that water which was required as its own means of accomplishment is specified as "moonlight itself is the water.
The meaning is that the water required here as the instrument for the sprinkling is nothing other than moonlight.

And it has been said: "Having made both of these [the object of comparison and the subject of comparison] subordinate members (*upasarjana*) in a compound, that which is subsequently expressed is one form of *rūpaka*; the other is what is called *samāsokti*.
Regarding the phrase "of both of these": [it refers to the object of comparison and the subject of comparison].
The meaning is "of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.
How then can it be said that, because of the predominance of the word *jyotsnā* (moonlight), the word *ambu* (water) is assumed to function figuratively (*guṇavṛtti*) by its influence?
It is replied:
In this case, indeed, two states exist:
first, the state of the moonlight being turned into water; second, the state of the moonlight, having been turned into water, consisting in its connection with the act of sprinkling.
In that case, when the moonlight first attains the state of water, then, because it is the subject under discussion (*prakaraṇika*), the moonlight is primary and the water is secondary by contrast.

At that time, the word "water" undergoes a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the moonlight, based on its association with qualities similar to the whiteness and so forth inherent in water, in accordance with the word "moonlight."

And at that time, because it conforms to the primary meaning [of the word "water"], its status as a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is stated by way of figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*). However, when this word *ambu* (water), having been made to assume the state of water so as to denote moonlight, attains connection with the act of sprinkling—
such that what is employed here as the means for sprinkling is not water but rather moonlight itself— and is thus qualified by moonlight, then...
It does not possess the state of a metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*),
because its qualities and functions have already been experienced in the prior state;
therefore, in that state, it partakes of the shadow of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
However, this is called *rūpaka* (metaphor) with reference to its previous state,
because it exists within the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) in accordance with the principal element (*pradhāna*).

Furthermore, the nature of being a *rūpaka* here should be understood as being literal (*anvartha*), since it consists in the endowment of the object that is the locus of superimposition with the form belonging to that which is being superimposed.

And here, through the perception of qualities similar to those residing in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the object being compared (*upameya*) of both the word and the form belonging to that object of comparison.
In this regard, there are three distinct views.
Some maintain that in this case, the superimposition of the meaning is preceded by the superimposition of the word.
Others, however, maintain that there is first the superimposition of the object and then the superimposition of the word;
yet others assert the simultaneity of the superimposition of the word and the superimposition of the object.
And this very position appears to be the more reasonable one.
Regarding this, they say:
"Some state that in a metaphor (*rūpaka*), that form [of the object] is expressed through the figurative application of the word;
others, however, maintain that it is the superimposition of the word [onto the object] based on the superimposition of that form."
But for those who perceive the qualities residing in the object of comparison as being equal to the qualities of the standard of comparison,
the form of that [standard] word appears there simultaneously.
Thus;
"therein" means "in the object of comparison."

Regarding the phrase "that nature of the word": this refers to the superimposition of the word of comparison (*upamāna-śabda*) and the superimposition of the form of the object compared (*upameya-rūpa*). Furthermore, that metaphor (*rūpaka*) is of two kinds.
One type [of suggestion] arises from the expression of every form through its own direct denotation (*svakaṇṭhena*).
As it has been said: "Since its composition is by means of direct audition (*śruti*), it therefore has all things as its object.
*Śruti* is the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) directed toward a continuous meaning; an example of this is what was stated beginning with "by the water of moonlight" (*jyotsnāmbunā*).
"Śārita" means variegated.

For here, among all those things— moonlight, the moon, stars, night, and the sky— which are presented as the subjects of comparison (*upameya*) by virtue of being "silver-like," their respective correlates— the water-jar, the flower, the maiden, and the garden— are explicitly stated (*svakaṇṭhena upātta*) as the objects of comparison (*rūpaka*), and there is no metaphorical identification of anything that is merely implied by the sense.
Therefore, in this case, the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇā*) occurs through hearing alone;
hence, it has all things as its object.
For here, all the things intended to be represented (*rūpyatvena abhimatāni vastūni*) are the objects of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) explicitly mentioned by its own name.
This is one type;

however, where there is a description of something partly by its own name and partly by implication, there is another type, consisting of a description through both direct statement (*śruti*) and implication (*artha*).
And in that regard, there is the state of being "turned" in one part, because it proceeds by means of a specific portion through its own explicit statement.
As it has been said: "And because its bondage [is established] both by scripture and by reasoning, it is therefore a partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivartin*).
An example of this is as follows:
"With peacock feathers, beautiful like young shoots, flying up and falling down..."
The kings of the lakes were fanned by royal swans, as if by the autumn season itself.
"Picchālyaḥ" refers to rows of feathers;
"rājahaṃsāḥ" refers to swans with red beaks and feet; "avījyanta" means they were fanned.

Although *vīji* is not listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*), it should be understood as having the meaning of "to fan," based on the usage of learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*), just like the words *milikhaci*, *klavi*, and *vikṣapi*.
Here, two forms of "shaping" (*rūpaṇa*) are explicitly stated by the author himself: "by those who are like young *picchāla* [birds] and *śāli* rice" and "the lake and the kings.
For instance, in one case, the *picchāla* birds are shaped by way of their being like young [children].
Elsewhere, however, the lakes are metaphorically represented as having the form of kings,
the royal swans as having the form of chowries, and autumn— the subject at hand— as having the form of a heroine; these [metaphors] are implied by the sense.
The meaning of the sentence here is that the autumnal lady, acting as the agent, fanned the kings of the lakes with royal swans that resembled chowries made of beautiful rows of feathers.
Thus, these two types of *rūpaka* (metaphor)—characterized as having all objects as its domain (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and as revolving around a single part (*ekadeśavivartin*)—have been described.

Alternatively, there is the state of having all objects as its domain for the *mālārūpaka* (garland-metaphor), for in that case, many metaphors are cast or projected together upon a single object of comparison (*rūpya*).
As it has been said:
"The *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor) is said to have all things as its object";
the word "or" (*yad vā*) is intended to introduce an alternative variety.

An illustration of this is as follows: The swarms of bees shone forth like the braided hair of the forest-deities, like chains of death for the wives of travelers, and like the sword-blades of the foremost warriors of Māra.
The "forest-edges" are the various regions of the forest;
the "braids" are masses of hair;
the "black chains" are the dragging chains employed by the God of Death.
The "heroic warriors of Māra" are the soldiers associated with Manmatha.
Here, three metaphors (*rūpaṇā*) are applied solely to the swarms of bees, which are presented as the objects of comparison, by means of expressions such as "the braids of the forest-deities.
Therefore, this constitutes the type where the metaphor applies to all the constituent elements (*samastavastuviṣayatā*).
Because many forms are cast together into a single form, it is a "partially manifest" (ekadeśavivartin) [metaphor], since it arises from being formed by means of another's form.
As it has been said: "It would be a partial occurrence because of being formed by another's form."
An illustration of this is as follows:
By means of white clouds, which illuminate the expanse of the sky with showers of rain like arrows, the kingdom of the quarters was brought into subjection.
"Āsāra" means a torrential downpour;
"viśikhāḥ" means arrows.
Here, the word *prasādhyate* functions through the shadow of paronomasia (*śleṣacchāyayā*) with respect to two meanings: "adornment" and "acquisition."
In this context, "ornament" (bhūṣaṇa) is the subject at hand; for it is the autumn season that is introduced here, and in that season,
the quarters of the sky are adorned by white clouds.
That which constitutes its acquisition is something else entirely, as it is not the subject under discussion here.

Regarding that other, non-contextual acquisition, there is a collection of causal factors (*kāraka-kadambaka*) by means of which it is described as having that form—namely, consisting of the king’s arrows, the kingdom, and the battlefield. By means of these, [the poet] sequentially [describes] the clouds, the showers, the rain-streaks, the directions, and the expanse of the sky.
The transformation (*rūpaṇā*) of those things intended as being "possessing form" (*rūpyatvena*) has been established;
therefore, in this case, there is the quality of residing in only one part (*ekadeśavṛttitva*).

For regarding the term *ekadeśavṛtti*, what is intended by the metaphor (*rūpaka*) is its residing in that sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) which is the sovereign lord (*īśaḥ prabhaviṣṇuḥ*) at one time (*ekadā*).
In his commentary on Bhāmaha’s definition of *viśeṣokti*, Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa has explained the term *ekadeśa* exactly as we have determined it; therein, the definition of *viśeṣokti* is as follows:

"When there is the disappearance of one part [of a whole], the praise of another quality for the purpose of manifesting a particular excellence is considered *viśeṣokti*, as for example: [followed by an illustration].

Therefore, here, just as in the definition of *viśeṣokti*, by the word "one part" (*ekadeśa*), the sentence-meaning—which is capable of manifesting at another time—is expressed; and elsewhere, the acquisition of that which is capable of manifesting at another time [is expressed].
For that [acquisition] is not the subject under discussion, yet it is brought here by virtue of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Therefore, in this case, there is occurrence in only one part.

The Illuminator (dīpaka): They know that to be the Illuminator where the objects of the beginning, middle, and end are connected to both the primary and the secondary [elements], with the common attribute of the simile contained within them. (UK 1.14)

Where there is the composition of such attributes (*dharma*) in which the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is internal and to be understood through the force of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthya*), there occurs the *kāvyadīpaka* (lamp of poetry).
And because the *dīpaka* has such poetry as its domain, that poetry is metaphorically called "the lamp" (*dīpaka*); thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In this case, it should be observed that the attributes are composed only once.
For he will explain the *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) when those [qualities] are mentioned more than once.

And for this very reason, even in the case of those qualities (*dharmas*) that reside in only one part [of the subject], when two sentence-meanings—or many such meanings—stand in the relation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), they possess the quality of being an illuminator (*dīpaka*) because they serve as the cause for illuminating that [object].

Furthermore, as long as those qualities are connected here through the integration of the relationship between the standard and object of comparison, it follows by necessity that they possess both primacy and subordination.
Because the object of comparison (upameya) is primary due to its topical relevance, whereas the standard of comparison (upamāna) is subordinate because it exists for the sake of that [object].
And thus, the phrase "possessing predominance and its opposite" here is a restatement (anuvāda),
because its meaning has already been established;
for "predominance" refers to primary status, and "its opposite" refers to non-predominance.
Those things which possess a connection or relation with those two are so described. Furthermore, this illuminator (dīpaka) is of three kinds,
because those attributes (dharmas) are composed as the objects of the initial, middle, and final sentences.
As it has been said: "Having as their objects the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Among these, an example of the *ādidīpaka* (illuminator at the beginning) is as follows:
"The autumn season withdrew the splendor of the kadamba flowers."
And for those separated from their beloveds, all their wealth of happiness has utterly vanished.

In this instance, the attribute consisting of withdrawal (*saṃharaṇa*)—being presented as having the beauty of the *kadamba* flower for its function and the destruction of the wealth of happiness of women separated from their lovers for its function—is an "internal simile" (*antargatopama*). Since the autumn season is being described, the withdrawal of the splendor of the *kadamba* flowers pertains to the contextual subject matter, whereas the withdrawal of the wealth of happiness of separated women pertains to a non-contextual subject matter; therefore, it is an internal simile here.
Just as [the autumn] completely took away the wealth of happiness for those separated from their beloveds, so too did it take away the splendor of the *kadamba* flowers.

Here, by means of the shadow of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the word "autumn" (*śaratkāla*) should be understood as referring to the "time of destruction" (*śaratsamaya*), colored by the sense of the "End-maker" (*antaka*, i.e., Death);
for the act of destruction is the work of the End-maker.

And here, because the word *saṃjahāra* (he withdrew), which is composed in the very first sentence, is sustained by the shadow of its recurrence (*anuṣaṅga*) in the second sentence, it constitutes the figure of *ādidīpaka* (illumination at the beginning).
An example of *madhyadīpaka* (illumination in the middle) is as follows:
"Dwelling in a foreign land, seeing people who have fallen from their status..."
And that autumn brought nothing but suffering to those away from home.

*Yātapatikāḥ* refers to women whose husbands have gone abroad; *proṣitabhartṛkāḥ* refers to those whose husbands are away. Since autumn is the subject under discussion (*prakaraṇika*), while the sight of women whose husbands are abroad living in a foreign land is not the subject, there is here an "internal simile" (*antargatopamā*). Furthermore, in this context, the sight of women whose husbands are abroad resulted solely in sorrow; thus, in the middle sentence, the property characterized as being the sole cause of suffering for those living abroad is introduced, which then [corresponds to] the two sentences at the beginning and the end.
It is employed as before;
by that, it serves as an illuminator of the middle.
An example of an illuminator at the end (antadīpaka) is as follows:
At that time, who was not filled with joy by both the moon of her beloved’s face— overflowing with the full radiance of its abundant beauty— and the [actual] moon?
At that time, during the autumn season;
here, the moon (*indu*) is the contextual subject (*prakaraṇika*), because it is the autumn season that is being described.
The moon-like face of the beloved (*kāntānanendu*), however, is non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*).
And since the fact that [the practice] is the cause of all happiness was established previously, it is relied upon here;
therefore, there is an "internal illuminator" (*antadīpaka*) here.
Thus has this *dīpaka* been defined and illustrated.

Now, an objection may be raised: since *upamā* (simile) was mentioned before *dīpaka* (the illuminator) in the statement "simile and the illuminator," then according to the maxim that "definition should follow the order of enumeration," the definition of *upamā* itself ought to have been given first, and that of *dīpaka* afterwards.
Why, then, has *dīpaka* been defined at the beginning? This must be explained.
It is said:
by this author, a portion of his own composition, the *Kumārasambhava*, has been presented here as an illustration;
for previously, examples of the *dīpaka* (illuminator) were given.

In this case, the order of enumeration has been abandoned so that there may be no interruption in the continuity of the investigation; however, the enumeration was not arranged in that manner for fear of breaking the metrical structure.
In the same way, regarding the subsequent characteristics as well, one should state that there is no fixed adherence to the order of the enumeration.
Simile (upamā)—
that which is a captivating commonality between the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameya),
expressed through words whose times and other attributes are mutually distinct, is simile. (UK 1.15)

Just as that [comparison] deserves syntactic connection through direct audition (*śruti*) by virtue of its association with the word *yathā*, it is said to be of two kinds: [that which arises] from the connection with words such as *sadṛśa* ("similar"), and otherwise.
Although this [simile] has been explained in brief by those who understand the terminology of similarity,
it is further established here through the exclusion of the common property (*sāmya*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and their respective designators (*tadvācin*).

When both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison are expressed, that [simile] occurs through the presence of the word expressing similarity; sometimes it occurs within a compound through the absence of that word expressing similarity, and sometimes it occurs even without it.
Likewise, by the force of the analogy and the statement regarding the *kyac* suffix [denoting habitual action],
in some cases that [action] belongs to the agent in the sense of habitual conduct (*ācāra*) through the *kyan* suffix, and in other cases it is expressed by the *kvip* suffix.
When the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a word meaning "excellent" (*kaṣādi*) with an object or an agent that functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
that [object] is expressed by the suffix *vat*, which denotes a commonality of action.
When a suffix such as *vat* is added to a noun ending in the sixth or seventh case to denote that very object,
it is employed by poets along with other secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *kalpa* and the like.
That which is contextual (prākaraṇika) and is presented as being connected by way of similarity is the object of comparison (upameya).
Indeed, even that which is contextual does not possess the status of the object of comparison if it is not presented as being connected by way of similarity,
just as in the case of the word "man" in the sentence, "Bring the king's man."

For in this case, although the *puruṣa* (the person) is part of the context (*prākaraṇika*), he is not the object of comparison (*upameya*) because he is being enjoined as something to be brought forth and is not presented as possessing a relationship of similarity.

Furthermore, even if there were a presentation based on a relationship of similarity, that which lacks contextual relevance would possess the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), not the status of the object of comparison; thus it is said to be "contextual" (*prākaraṇika*).
Thus, that which is contextual (prākaraṇika) and is presented as being connected through similarity is the object of comparison (upameya).
For it is cast into proximity by means of the presentation of similarity with the standard of comparison (upamāna); therefore, it is the upameya.
But that which is non-contextual (aprākaraṇika), being of the same nature, is the standard of comparison (upamāna).

The commonality (*sādharmya*) between those two—the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*)—is the shared attribute; the connection through that attribute is *upamā* (simile), because it serves as the cause for determining proximity by means of the similarity between the object of comparison and the object compared. Furthermore, its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is already established by virtue of its inclusion in the section on ornaments, since those properties which bring beauty to poetry, being distinct from the *guṇas*, constitute ornaments.
Indeed, *guṇas* (qualities) are those attributes that are the causes of the beauty of poetry;

they are characterized by *mādhurya* (sweetness), *ojas* (vigour), and *prasāda* (clarity). However, those which serve as the cause for an excellence of beauty in poetry whose beauty has already been produced by the *guṇas* are *alaṅkāras* (ornaments).
As Bhaṭṭa Vāmana said:
"Qualities (guṇas) are those attributes that produce the beauty of poetry;
figures of speech (alaṅkāras) are the causes of its excellence. Thus, by virtue of being a figure of speech, the charm of the simile is already established;
therefore, the phrase "captivating the heart" is a restatement (anuvāda).
Because the meaning is already established;
furthermore, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison does not occur through absolute similarity when [the words] are employed, as in the case of "this cow is like a cow.
Therefore, it was said: "between two words whose times and other attributes are mutually distinct."
In this context, time and so forth are intended as the grounds for the application of words.
Indeed, for certain words functioning in their own primary sense, time is the ground for their application, as is the case with words such as "spring" (*vasanta*) and the like.
For some, it is direction, as in the case of the east and so forth;
for others, it is genus, as in the case of cows and so forth.
In the case of "white" and so forth, it is a quality (*guṇa*);
in the case of "goes" and so forth, it is an action (*kriyā*);
and in the case of "the king's man" and so forth, it is a relationship (*saṃbandha*), such as that between owner and owned.
In this way, other cases should also be understood accordingly.

"Mutually distinct" refers to time and so forth; "of which two words" means those two words that have such [factors] as their grounds for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*); and "of which two [objects], the standard of comparison and the object of comparison" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.
However, when one says "this is a cow" (gaur ayam gauḥ), there is no difference in the ground for the application [of the term],
because the single property of cowness (gotva) alone serves as that ground.
Therefore, such a relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison does not exist.
In the sentence "But that is simile" (*upamā tu tat*), the word "but" (*tu*) refers to the distinction from other figures of speech;
the meaning is that "simile, moreover, is of this kind.
And this simile is twofold.
It is both complete (*pūrṇā*) and elliptical (*luptā*).

The complete [simile] is that in which four elements are employed: the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), their common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) such as beauty, and a particle such as *iva* that indicates the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison. Furthermore, that complete [simile] is of three kinds.
This is because [the *upamā*] is determined through sentences (*vākya*), compounds (*samāsa*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

Among these, that which is determined through a sentence is twofold, distinguished by being either directly expressed (*śrauta*) or implied (*ārtha*). That which is determined through an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is the directly expressed (*śrautī*) [type].

For an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by virtue of having its case-endings elided, does not rest upon either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone; rather, it illuminates the relationship between both the standard and the object of comparison—consisting of the states of object (*karman*) or instrument (*karaṇa*) as appropriate—as being the objective domain of the act of comparison (*upamitikriyā*).
Therefore, in that case, the simile is based on a direct word (*śrautī upamā*).
As it has been said:
"Just as [a word] through its connection with *yathā* or *iva* deserves syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by means of direct audition (*śruti*)."

In this context, the words *yathā* and *iva* are merely illustrative; for even from other indeclinables such as *vā* and so forth, the relationship of comparison between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood in that same manner.
For example: [text follows].
Know her to be one of few words, my very second life,
like a solitary female cakravāka bird when I, her companion, have gone far away—
a young woman of intense longing as these heavy days pass by.
I think she has become like a lotus-pond withered by the cold, transformed into something else entirely.

In that regard, an example of that [simile] in connection with the word *yathā* is as follows: "For the separated lovers, the lunar light became like sandalwood—for a moment it served to rouse the fever of passion, and subsequently to increase their torment. (Udbhaṭa Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha 1.18)
In this instance, the lunar light is the object of comparison (upameya) and the sandalwood paste is the standard of comparison (upamāna).
The common attribute (sādhāraṇa-dharma)— the state of being the cause for the arising of the fever of passion and the basis for the increase of torment— is not fixed [to either one alone].

Since the word *yathā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and thus lacks an explicit case-ending, it rests upon the meaning of either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*); yet, by its very nature as a verbal particle (*śrauta*), it illuminates the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) which is based on both.
Therefore, this is a complete simile (*saṃpūrṇā*) and is verbal (*śrautī*).
An example should be applied in the same way for the use of the word *iva*.
With their blue lotuses like eyes, their lotuses like faces,
and their ruddy geese like breasts, the glories of the lakes shone like young women.
Thus, this complete sentence simile (vākyopamā), shown with the word *iva*, has been described as being based on the Vedic usage (*śrautī*).

However, in that [simile] which is joined by words such as *sadṛśa* ("similar") and so forth, the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is not understood through the form of the Vedic usage— that is, by following both terms through the word *iva*— but rather through the sense (*artha*).
Because words such as "sadṛśa" (similar) rest upon the identity of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison in one place alone,
yet in another place they are understood to be related to them through the consideration of the similarity residing therein;
therefore, this [simile] is based on meaning (ārthī).
Thus it has been said: "Because of the connection with words such as 'similar' (sadṛśa), otherwise.
"Otherwise" means in a manner that is not based on the literal sense (aśrauta).

An example of this is as follows: "At night, the grove of white water-lilies, bright from its blossoming and with bees settled upon the filaments, resembled the orb of the full moon. (Udbhaṭa Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha 1.20)
In this instance, the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is the blooming lily grove, characterized by bees settled upon its filaments; the moon’s orb is the object of comparison (*upamāna*);
and whiteness is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).

The word *pratimā* is the cause for the comprehension of the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), and it finds its final rest in the standard of comparison. For instance:
In this case, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed as "that which has an image resembling the full moon's orb. Thus, the word *pratimā* (image) rests upon the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
And by that [word] resting upon the standard of comparison, the similarity of the object being compared (*upameya*) is understood by implication.
This is because similarity resides in both [the object of comparison and the standard of comparison].

Furthermore, even when there is a *tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound such as "a likeness by means of the full orb of the moon" (*pūrṇendubimbena pratima*), the similarity is expressed directly by its own name (*svakaṇṭhena*) in the object of comparison (*upameya*),
while in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is understood by implication.

Therefore, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) is understood through a consideration of the similarity residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); whereas in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the understanding of the standard of comparison as a standard arises from an investigation of the similarity residing in the object of comparison. This is the implied meaning of the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison here.

Furthermore, by the power of the expression "the bees clinging to the filaments residing in the object of comparison," another point of commonality not explicitly stated—namely, the quality of having a dark interior—is also suggested.
Just as the orb of the full moon has a dark interior because of the mark of the hare, so too the grove of night-lotuses has a dark interior because of the bees settled upon its filaments.
Therefore, with respect to the attribute characterized by having a dark interior, this is a "defective" (luptā) simile because one part [of the comparison] is omitted.

However, in cases such as "as if with eyes that are blue lotuses," although there are common attributes such as length and blueness shared by the eyes and the lotuses, etc., [the comparison remains complete].
Although they are not expressed by their own specific words, nevertheless, because they enter into the meaning being denoted as it is being described, the simile remains complete,
since all four components are perceived;
for the eyes and so forth are the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) here.
The lotus and so forth are the objects of comparison (upameya);
the common property (sādhāraṇadharma) extends to the qualifiers such as "shining," "long," and "blue";
and the word "iva" is the cause for the comprehension of the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva).
Therefore, this simile is indeed complete; however, because of its dark interior, it is described as being "omitted" (lupta) in comparison to the white [moon].
This is also a compound simile (*samāsopamā*), because the compound "resembling the orb of the full moon" (*pūrṇendubimbapratimam*) has been prescribed.
But when a sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) is intended here, then this very same example serves as an illustration for that purpose.
The forest of beautiful waters was like the unbroken moon.
In this way, it should be dedicated.
Thus, this complete simile, which is understood through syntactical construction, has been presented as twofold—verbal (*śrautī*) and objective (*ārthī*)—along with its varieties such as *pratīpa*.
However, that which is understood through compound formation is stated to be of only one kind, namely the objective (*ārthī*).

As for that [simile] which is understood through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and is complete, it too is twofold, distinguished by being either expressed by a word (*śrauta*) or implied by the sense (*ārtha*).

In this regard, the *vat* suffix prescribed by the rule "tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116) serves as the basis for the comprehension of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison by way of following both [terms], because it is prescribed in the sense of "like" (*iva*), and thus possesses a verbal form (*śrauta-rūpa*) identical to the word "iva" itself.

Furthermore, when the suffix *vat* is prescribed in the sense of "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), as in "the Kṣatriya studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyam adhīte brāhmaṇavad adhīte kṣatriyaḥ*), the equality— which, by means of the action of studying, ultimately rests upon the object of comparison (*upameya*)— is understood through reflection on that [equality] to imply, by implication, the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Therefore, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison exists there.
As it has been said:
"By means of the suffix -vat, which expresses a commonality of action..."
Furthermore, regarding the rule "the suffix *vat* [is used] after a word ending in the sixth or seventh case when it denotes a name, provided that [the name] is what is to be expressed":

the suffix *vat* expresses a general action, because it is prescribed for the equality of actions in the rule "when there is equality with that [in respect of an action], the suffix *vat* [is used]" (Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.115).
And by that [suffix], the simile (*upamā*) is expressed.
The term "vācyā" (expressed), which was introduced previously, is connected here.
The grammatical connection is: from a noun—that is, from a nominal stem—ending in the sixth case or the seventh case.
In that regard, an example of the first [type] is as follows:
"Could that fair-faced woman perhaps somehow stand within the path of my vision,
having arrived unasked, like a rain from a cloudless sky falling upon one who has fallen?"
The connection is that she, having arrived unbidden, might somehow remain fallen within the range of his vision;
here, "unclouded rain" is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and "the fair-faced one" is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
When [the object] has arrived unasked, its remaining within the range of vision is the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharma*).

And the suffix *vati*, being prescribed for the equality of action, comes to rest through the word and the operation via the action in the object of comparison (*upameya*); then, by reflecting upon that equality, it makes known the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as the standard of comparison.
Thus, in this case, the relationship of standard and object of comparison is understood through the sense (*artha*).
Therefore, this [type of *arthāntaranyāsa*] is complete; it is to be understood through the use of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
An example of the second type is as follows:
"Would there not be unrestrained yearnings for her as well, just as mine?"
They were brought about by that wretched god of love, who acts with such sudden and violent ferocity.
*Akāṇḍoḍḍāmaro* means "fierce out of season" or "sudden and violent";
*pracaṇḍa* is an alternative reading.
*Utkalikāḥ* refers to longings or yearnings.
In this context, the referent of "we" (asmad-artha) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); the referent of "that" (*tad-śabda-artha*) is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Those unrestrained yearnings (*utkalikā*) bestowed by the God of Love constitute the agent; their "coming into being" (*bhavana*) is the common property (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*).

The suffix *vat*—because it is prescribed in the sense of "as if," like the word *iva*—does not rest upon either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*), but rather indicates the relationship of comparison itself through its literal form.
Therefore, this [type of simile] is complete, expressed by a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and is *śrautī* (based on the literal sense).
However, in the reading *tasyā api* (of that also), the suffix *vati* is prescribed after a word ending in the genitive case.
But when the reading is *tasyām api*, then it is derived from a locative ending.
As it has been stated: "The doubt that exists regarding the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is excluded by the object of comparison (*upameya*), and so forth.
Thus, this complete simile, which is threefold and is to be understood through sentences, compounds, and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), has been explained.

In that regard, it has been stated that the two types of simile—those determined by a sentence (*vākya*) and those determined by a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—each have a twofold division based on the distinction between being expressed directly (*śrauta*) or implied (*ārtha*). However, that which is determined by a compound (*samāsa*) is exclusively implied (*ārtha*).
Therefore, this [simile] is complete in five varieties.
That which is a "deleted simile" (*luptopamā*) because one part has been omitted is the "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*).

It is of five kinds, according as it is understood through a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), a nominal stem (*subanta*), a verbal root (*dhātu*), or a primary or secondary derivative (*kṛt* and *taddhita*).
Among these, the abbreviated simile occurring in a sentence was illustrated previously with the example: "equal to the unbroken moon."

For here, because the state of having a dark belly (*asitodaratva*) is not explicitly mentioned and the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not employed, there is also the presence of "elliptical partiality" (*luptaikadeśatva*).
Furthermore, the abbreviated simile (*saṃkṣepopamā*), which is to be understood through compound (*samāsa*), is of three kinds,
owing to its occurrence when one, two, or all three [elements] are omitted.
When one [of the two] is omitted, there are two types:
[the first] due to the non-employment of "iva" and so forth, which express a common attribute; as it has been said: "when that which expresses similarity is absent."
And [the phrase] "in the absence of a word expressing that" means:
that which expresses similarity is that which expresses the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).
(The common property)
Beauty and so forth;
and the words expressing that, such as *iva* and others, which express the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).
And in this entire section, [it is understood] that "even though this has not been stated in detail."
The three terms— “in some cases,” “compound,” and “is composed”— are each to be supplied as appropriate to the context.

In that regard, as for the "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) which occurs within a compound through the omission of a word expressing similarity, an example of it has already been stated previously: "resembling the orb of the full moon.
For here, the quality of having a dark interior is not expressed by a word, as it is understood through the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*).
Now, an example of that [type of *śleṣa*] occurring in separation from the letter *v* and others is as follows:
"At that time, amidst a multitude of *kādamba* birds warbling with agitation, Dhūrjaṭi—the tiger among the lords of the gods—[was overcome] by remorse. (Udbhaṭa, Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha 1.24)
He set his mind upon that Gaurī, whose face was like the moon’s radiance, whose eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, and who was as fair as the pericarp of a lotus.
*Kādambas* are a species of birds.
In the phrase "Gaurī, who is fair as the pericarp of a lotus," the lotus pericarp (*sarojakarṇikā*) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
and Gaurī is the object of comparison (*upameyā*).

Whiteness (*gauratva*) is the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). These three [elements] are explicitly mentioned by the author himself. However, as for the meaning of "as" (*iva*) and so forth, it is governed by the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55), which concerns the word expressing the common property used together with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Thus, it is understood through the force of that compound that this [simile] is one whose parts are elided due to the omission of words such as "iva" (like).
In this way, when there is a single elision, the simile within a compound is said to be of two kinds.

But when both [the word for the common property and the particle] are omitted, it becomes of a single type, because both the word expressing the common property and the particle *iva* are simultaneously not employed.

As it has been said: "When both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison are mentioned, [it is a case of *luptopamā*] due to the absence of the word for similarity and its expresser. In this regard:
By the word "sāmya" (similarity), a word expressing similarity is indicated;
for since comparison is impossible without similarity, its example is: "O tiger among the lords of the thirty [gods]."

And in the phrase "one whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus," and in the phrase "the tiger among the lords of the thirty [gods]," the lord of the thirty is the object of comparison (upameya) and the tiger is the standard of comparison (upamāna).
And that pair [of comparison and similarity] is expressed by its own throat [i.e., directly].
The meaning of "as if" (iva) and so forth, as well as the common property such as brilliance and the like, are understood through implication.
However, in the case of "her eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus," the petals of the blue lotus function as the standard of comparison (upamāna).

The eyes are the objects of comparison (*upameya*), and these two are explicitly mentioned by their own names. The common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), such as blueness or length, as well as the sense of "like" (*iva*) and so forth—which constitutes the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—is not expressed by its own word; nevertheless, it is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*) by virtue of the compound.
However, there is a distinction between *tridaśādhīśaśārdūla* and *nīlotpaladalekṣaṇām* caused by their respective grammatical structures as bahuvrīhis;
for in the latter case, a tatpuruṣa compound is prescribed by the rule "an object compared [is compounded] with *vyāghra* and so forth.

Thus, because of the absence of both the word expressing the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and the particle *iva*, this is called an "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) within a compound where two elements are elided.

But when all three [elements] are omitted, there occurs an "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) existing within a compound, due to the simultaneous non-employment of words such as *iva* that express the common property, the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the relationship between the standard and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*).
As it has been said: "And because of the absence of the similarity, the object of comparison, and the word expressing them.
Here too, as before, by the words "similarity" (*sāmya*) and "object of comparison" (*upameya*), the words expressing those are indicated through metonymy (*lakṣyate*).
An example of this is: "śaśicchāyavadanām" (one whose face has the luster of the moon).

For here, within a *bahuvrīhi* compound that contains another *bahuvrīhi*, the phrase "whose face has a luster equal to the moon's" indicates that the moon's radiance is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the radiance of the face is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Furthermore, a fourfold set is understood: the two [objects] themselves, their common property such as "delightfulness," and their equality.
