However, it is only the simile (*upamāna*) that is directly touched by the word, namely "moon-like" (*śaśicchāya*).
This is because the other three—the object of comparison (*upameya*) and so forth—are to be understood through the sense (*artha*), by virtue of the power of the compound.
Thus, this *saṃkṣepopamā* (abbreviated simile), which occurs when three [elements] are omitted, has been illustrated.
In this way, the four types of *luptā-samāsopamā* (elliptical compound similes) have been explained here:
two in which one element is omitted, and so forth.
There is one type when two elements are elided,
and another when three are elided.
Furthermore, simile derivable from nominal stems and verbal roots (*subdhātu*) is of three kinds, because it is derivable from the suffixes *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *kvip*.
The *kyac* suffix is also understood to be threefold, depending on whether the object (*karman*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
As it has been said: "Likewise, by the force of the *kyac* suffix, [the suffix] is stated when there is conduct based on a standard of comparison.
Just as in a compound (*samāsa*), a simile expressed in an abbreviated form is employed because it is understood through the power of the compound itself, so too [is it here].

In a certain context, by the force of the *kyac* suffix— both that prescribed in the sūtra and that added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyānika*)— which respectively follows from the sense of analogy (*upamāna*) when the object (*karman*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended in the sense of habitual practice (*ācāra*), that very expression which is thus determined is also composed [as a poetic figure]. An example of it is as follows:
Though he had accomplished his purpose and possessed the entirety of sovereign splendor,
he felt as if he were in hell within that forest, which was most intensely desirable.
The connection is: "even though he has achieved his purpose through the perfection of all sovereign powers.

Here, the phrase "acting as if his own self were in a state of distress" indicates that someone afflicted by poverty and so forth is the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison), while the Self of the Blessed One is the *upameya* (the object of comparison).
The common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) called "conduct" (*ācāra*) is expressed by the *kyac* suffix.
Here, both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the common attribute are directly touched by the word;
the object of comparison (*upameya*), as well as the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison, is understood through implication (*sāmarthyāt*).
Thus, because the meaning of the two [elements] is understood and the two are elided, this is a *subdhātūpamā* (simile based on verbal roots).
In this way, this *subdhātūpamā* having an object (*karman*) as its point of comparison has been illustrated.
However, one having a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its point of comparison is exemplified by: "He behaves like a denizen of hell in the forest" (*narakīyati kānane*).
In this instance, "hell" (naraka) is the standard of comparison (upamāna), "the forest" (kānana) is the object of comparison (upameya),
and "conduct" (ācāra)— which is conveyed by the suffix *kyac*— is the common attribute (sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ).

However, particles such as *iva* and the like are not employed here because the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is to be understood through the power of the suffix *kyac*.
Therefore, when there is an elision of one [of the two], this is a "compound-based simile" (*subdhātūpamā*).
Thus, this twofold abbreviated simile (*saṃkṣepopamā*), which is to be understood through the suffix *kyac*, has been described.
However, when understood through the force of the *kyaṅ* suffix, there occurs a "concise simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) which has the agent as its standard of comparison.
Thus it is said: "By means of *kyaṅ*, [the suffix] *se* is applied in the sense of the agent’s conduct," and likewise, "in that manner."
Regarding the rule "upamānād ācāre" (Pāṇini 3.1.10),

the phrase "in some cases" (kvacit) from the preceding [sūtra] is to be supplied here. The meaning is that in certain instances, a "concise simile" (saṃkṣepopamā) is composed by means of the suffix *kyaṅ*, which follows a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and pertains to the domain of conduct (*ācāra*).
An illustration of this is as follows:
For him who beheld the world as being like fire in the absence of his beloved, the great festival of the knowledge of reality began to act like a mere glow-worm.
*Khadyota* means a garland of light.
Here, in expressions such as "to act like a firefly" (*khadyotāyitum*), the firefly (*khadyota*) serves as the standard of comparison.
*Tattvajñāna* (knowledge of reality) is the precise determination of the true nature of things.
That which consists of that [nature] is "mahat," meaning excellent; it is comparable to "mahaḥ," which means splendor.

The suffix *kyaṅ* conveys the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), namely the conduct [of the two]. Because this is understood through the power of the suffix *kyaṅ*, particles such as *itra* are not employed.

Therefore, this *saṃkṣepopamā* (abbreviated simile), composed by means of a single elision (*ekalopa*) and comparable to the *subdhātu* suffixes, is in certain instances formed with the *kvip* suffix, where the agent and the object of comparison are identical. And that *kvip* is prescribed by the rule: "The *kvip* suffix may optionally be applied after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kvibvā vaktavyaḥ*)."
As it has been said: "In some cases, that [suffix] is formed with *kvip*";
here too it is the same, according to the rule "from a standard of comparison, the suffix expressing habitual behavior."
The phrase "of the agent" (kartuḥ) is to be supplied to all three [types of comparison].
An example of that is:
"The world is like fire; this world is comparable [to it]."
And common conduct (*ācāra*) is understood as the shared property (*dharma*) by the force of the *kvip* suffix.

In this case, because the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are expressed by words, while the verbal activity (*ivādi*) and the conduct are to be determined by the force of the meaning, there is an elision of that pair.
Indeed, it is impossible to claim that the unexpressed *kvip* possesses the capacity to denote a meaning.
Thus, this threefold abbreviated simile is to be understood as being determined by the suffixes *kyac*,
*kyaṅ*, and *kvip*; however,
that which is determined by the power of the *kyac* suffix is twofold.
Because it functions as a comparison based on action and locus,
that which is understood through the *kyap* suffix is of one kind,
and that which is understood through the *kvip* suffix is likewise of only one kind.
Thus, this fourfold abbreviated simile, to be understood through nominal suffixes (*sub-dhātu-pratyaya*), has been explained in brief.

The abbreviated simile to be understood through the force of verbal suffixes (*kṛt-pratyaya*) is twofold: that which has an object as its point of comparison (*karma-upamānika*) and that which has an agent as its point of comparison (*kartṛ-upamānika*).

Thus it has been said: "That [suffix] *ṇamul* which occurs after roots such as *kaṣ* when there is an object of comparison, whether in the sense of an object (*karman*) or an agent (*kartṛ*), denotes that [object]. The phrase "occurring after roots such as *kaṣ*" means "having the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of roots such as *kaṣ*.
An example of this when the object of comparison is an object (*karma*) is as follows:
The fire of passion blazed within his mind, burning it with the heat of a mental fever for her;
his intellect was drawn toward Umā by the power of his asceticism.
In this context, the mind belonging to the other, the ordinary person, is the standard of comparison (upamāna);
the mind of the Blessed One is the object of comparison (upameya);
and the state of being burned is the common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma).
And that triad is touched upon by the word.

However, the relationship of similarity between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is understood here through the force of the suffix *ṇamul*, even in the absence of words such as *iva* and so forth.

Therefore, this is an "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) involving the elision of one term; it has the object of comparison as its basis and is to be understood through a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*).

An illustration of that [simile] based on the agent is as follows: "Even with his body burnt away, his self remaining only through the persistence of his vigor, he, touched by desire, thought a thought common to ordinary beings. (UK 1.29)
"Vigraha" means body.
Here, a living being who is merely common and devoid of any excellence of qualities is the "upamāna" (the standard of comparison),
while the Blessed One, indicated by that term, is the "upameya" (the object of comparison).
The quality of being a thinker (*cintayitṛtva*) is a common attribute;
and by the force of the suffix *ṇamul*, even in the absence of words such as *iva* and so forth, the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is determined.

Therefore, when there is an elision of one element, this is a "contracted simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) in which the agent serves as the standard of comparison, and it is to be understood through the *kṛt* suffix.

Thus, this abbreviated simile (saṃkṣepopamā), which is to be understood through the formation of primary and secondary suffixes, has been explained as being of two kinds. As for that which is to be understood through the power of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and is comprehended from the word *vati*, it was mentioned first because it is complete.
But another [type of *upamā*] is incomplete; it is understood from its usage with secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) such as *kalpa* and so forth.
As it has been said: "That [simile] is composed by poets using *kalpa* and other secondary derivatives.

Here, by the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), there is the inclusion of suffixes such as *kan*, which are prescribed by rules beginning with "in the sense of a likeness, [the suffix *kan* is added]" (*ive pratikṛtau*).
An example of this is as follows:
"Now that I have vanished, appearing like a Caṇḍāla and consumed by the god of love, she has fallen into incomparable despair; could she perhaps have died from grief?"
In this [verse], the *caṇḍāla* is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), "in me" (*mayi*)— the referent of the first-person pronoun— is the object of comparison (*upameya*),
and similarity is conveyed by the suffix *-kalpa*.

According to the view of the venerable Kātyāyana, since suffixes such as *kalpa* are prescribed for a meaning similar to the sense of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*), cruelty and so forth—though not explicitly conveyed by their own words—are understood here through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*).
Therefore, when there is an elision of one [of the two members], this is a "concise simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) to be understood from a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
This should be understood in the same way regarding the example *aśvaka*.
Because the suffix *kan* is prescribed for a similar object characterized by the sense of "as it were" (*iva*),
whereas in cases such as *āyaḥśūlika*, the understanding of the simile arises through the power of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) by means of the elision of the three [elements].
For instance, having analyzed the compound here as *ayaḥśūlena anvicchati* ("he seeks with an iron spike"), the suffix *ṭhak* is enjoined by the rule *ayaḥśūla-daṇḍājina-bhyām*.

In this instance, four elements are understood: the iron spike as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), some means of seeking out an object as the subject of comparison (*upameya*), the common property such as sharpness, and the relationship between the standard and the subject of comparison.
Among these, the iron spike is explicitly expressed by its own word (*svaśabda-sphuṭa*) as the standard of comparison.

However, the meaning of the three remaining words is understood here through the force of the context. Now, one might object: since here the means of seeking the object (the iron spear) is perceived as non-different from the object of comparison (the simile) by means of identifying it with the state of that [object], this is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and not *upamā* (simile). Therefore, how can this be an example of *upamā*?
It is said:

just as in the case of the expression "her face with the luster of the moon," although the luster of the face is not actually covered by the moon's luster, the status of this as a distinct type of simile is proposed by first establishing some manner of perceived difference; so too it will be here, and thus there is no fault.

Therefore, in the case of *ayaḥ-śūlika* ("iron-spiked"), when the three [elements] are elided, there occurs an "abbreviated simile" (*saṃkṣepopamā*) to be understood through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). Likewise, in cases such as *śvā mumūrṣati* ("the dog wishes to die") and *kūlaṃ pipatipati* ("the bank wishes to fall"), if—due to the superimposition (*adhyavasāna*) of that state upon the object of comparison (the dog or the bank) which possesses qualities conducive to dying or falling—the intended identity with the standard of comparison (death or falling), expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), is perceived as being brought about by that desire; [then this is also an abbreviated simile].
If there exists some basis for the apprehension of a distinction [between the two], then it should be stated that this is a variety of *upamā* (simile).
Otherwise, however, it is to be understood as a variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

As the venerable Kātyāyana stated in his *Vārttika* on the rules for the suffix *san*: “An addition must be made regarding insentient objects when there is a possibility [of such apprehension]; or rather, it is not necessary, because since the cause is the same, the perception [of the action] arises from the activity of desire.”
And regarding the statement, "Or it is established through analogy," here, by the phrase "or rather, because the causes are similar," etc., the determination of its existence is indicated;
whereas by "or it is established through analogy," the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is set forth.

And this [example] is to be understood as a type of *dhātūpamā* (simile of verbal roots), because the suffix *san* is prescribed after a root (*ghātoḥ*) and that which ends in it is also a root, just like the *subdhātūpamā*.

In the same way, in cases such as "proximity to the present" (*vartamānasāmīpya*), one should apply the classification as either a variety of *upamā* or a variety of *atiśayokti* according to how they are perceived.
However, for the author of the *Cūrṇi*, in such instances, because he relies on the identification (*adhyavasāna*) with that state, he does not accept them as varieties of *atiśayokti*.
As it has been said: "There is no simile with a finite verb.

For this very reason, Daṇḍin, in such passages as "Darkness, as if smearing the limbs; the sky, as if raining collyrium; vision has become fruitless, as if through service to a wicked man," explained at great length that these are indeed instances of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) wherein the *atiśaya* (exaggeration) is internalized (*garbhīkṛta*).

Therefore, even in cases such as "Devadatta, when will you go to the village? or "I am going now," since the future time is determined as having the form of the present due to its proximity to the present (*vartamānasāmīpya*), it must be stated that this is indeed a variety of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole).
This should be inferred in other instances as well.

Thus, this concise simile (saṃkṣepopamā), which is to be understood through sentences, compounds, verbal roots, primary suffixes (kṛt), and secondary suffixes (taddhita), has been explained as being of five kinds.
However, the complete simile (sampūrṇopamā) was previously stated to be of three kinds, distinguished by sentences, compounds, and secondary suffixes.
Furthermore, other intermediate subdivisions of these very types have been specified.

For instance, it has been stated that complete *vākya-upamā* (sentence simile) and *taddhita-upamā* (secondary derivative simile) each have two varieties, distinguished by being expressed through words (*śrauta*) or through meaning (*ārtha*).
Furthermore, *saṃkṣepa-upamā* (abbreviated simile) and *samāsa-upamā* (compound simile) each have four varieties, based on the elision of one, two, or three [elements].
Indeed, it has been stated therein that the elision of one element has two varieties.

Due to the elision of the particle *iva* and the word expressing the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), there are four types of verbal simile (*sabdhātūpamā*), as they are to be understood through the suffixes *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *kvip*. Indeed, that which is to be understood through the *kyac* suffix is said to be of two kinds, according to whether the object (*karman*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Furthermore, that which is to be determined through the suffixes of the *kṛt* class is twofold, by virtue of having an agent (*kartṛ*), an object (*karman*), or a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as its correlate.
Thus, this seventeenfold simile has been expounded by the author of the treatise. As they say:

Simile is understood to be of two kinds— complete and with a missing element— from primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), verbal roots (*subdhātu*), or from a sentence (*vākya*).
"By the elision of one, two, or three [elements], there would be three types of *lopinī* (elliptical expressions);
here, the first two varieties are twofold, while the third is of a single form.

Thus, regarding the phrase "the first two varieties are twofold," there is a twofold nature of the single elision (*ekalopa*) resulting from the elision of the word expressing the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

The elision of two [terms] is also twofold: first, due to the absence of the word expressing the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and second, due to the absence of the word expressing the object of comparison (*upameya*).
And it has been stated that although this simile possesses various distinct varieties, it attains the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) only where there is a captivating charm, not everywhere.
Prativastūpamā (The Simile by Corresponding Objects):

Where, in the proximity of the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the expression of similarity is uttered by the wise, and where the object of comparison (*upameya*) is [also] mentioned by poets—that is called *prativastūpamā*. (UK 1.22)
Where, in the proximity of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), a word expressing similarity is employed more than once, that is *parivastūpamā*.
Now, if a word expressing similarity is employed there more than once, would it not follow that there is a plurality of sentences?
And yet, words such as *iva* and so forth are not employed within more than one sentence.
Because their capacity for denotation is determined by their subsistence within a single sentence;

therefore, having raised the objection—"In the absence of words such as *iva*, how can the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) be determined there?"—he says:
"And [the word] attains the status of the object of comparison by virtue of its position as either the contextual or the non-contextual."
And "another" [is] the state of being a standard of comparison; thus, there is an absence of words expressing a simile.

The meaning is that even when words such as "like" (*iva*) and so forth are not employed, the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is determined here through the power of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*), by considering what is relevant to the context (*prākaraṇika*) and what is not.
As they say:
"In some cases, even though [words] such as *iva* are not perceived, [the comparison arises] from the refinement of the word (*śabdasaṃskāra*)."
"Elsewhere, simile is perceived as being based solely on the meaning.
Thus, here, the apprehension of simile occurs through three modes:
in some cases, by the power of words such as *iva* and others, the simile is understood as being directly expressed (*vācyabhūtā*).
As in "her face is like the moon" and so forth;

however, in some cases, that [indication] is understood through the mediation of the expression of its own primary meaning, arising from a word assisted by the specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) associated with each [particular instance],
as in "dark as a sword-blade."
For here,
by means of the two words *śastrī* (knife) and *śyāmā* (dark), which are accompanied by the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of forming a single compound through the rules of *samāsa*,
the suggested simile (*upamā*) is understood through the mediation of the denotation of their own respective meanings.

In some cases, however, even in the absence of verbal refinement based on the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is a comprehension of that [comparison] from the power of the meaning alone, as in the case of metaphors (*rūpaka*), illuminators (*dīpaka*), and "counter-fact simile" (*prativastūpamā*).
Therefore, in this *prativastūpamā*, the status of being the standard and the object of comparison is understood through the power of the meaning alone; thus, there is no fault.

An example of this is as follows: "Rare in this world are such perfections of character and beauty; how few nights are there even in a year when the moon appears with its full orb? (Udbhaṭasāgara-kāvya 1.31)
"Rare" means very few.
"Such as those existing in Pārvatī" refers to those perfections of character and beauty that resemble hers.
"Character" (*śīla*) means a virtuous nature.
Beauty is loveliness.
Here, the twelve nights within the year that possess the form of the unbroken lunar disc serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
The collections of virtue and beauty, which are preeminent among all people yet possessed by only a few individuals, are the objects of comparison (*upameya*).
And the common property is "scarcity. This is expressed as "how many" when in proximity to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
but as "rare" when in proximity to the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Moreover, even in the absence of words such as "iva" (like), the determination of the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison occurs through a consideration of what is contextual and what is not.
Therefore, this is *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence), because it is based on the connection of common attributes to each respective thing.
Thus ends the first section in the *Laghuvṛtti* on the *Udbhaṭālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious Pratīhāra Indurāja.
Now begins the second section:
Paraleipsis (*ākṣepa*), Corroboration by another matter (*arthāntaranyāsa*), Contrast (*vyatireka*), and Peculiar Causation (*vibhāvanā*).
Others recognize the figures of speech as Samāsa (Condensation) and Atiśayokti (Hyperbole).

In the phrase "and *samāsātiśayoktī*," the word *ukti* (expression) is connected individually with each of the words *samāsa* (compression) and *atiśaya* (exaggeration). *Ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is that which is like a negation of something intended [to be said], for the purpose of expressing a specific distinction.
The wise and learned poets always praise that which is called "inspiration."
In this context, there occurs a certain type of indirect speech (*vakrabhaṇiti*) in which the intended meaning is refined by means of a negation,
yet it is not actually negated.
In that case, the negation that is performed regarding the intended meaning becomes, as it were, a mere semblance of a negation.
But it is not merely a negation;
for the sentence does not terminate there, since that [negation] constitutes the meaning of a subordinate clause.
And the status of being the meaning of a subordinate clause arises because the negation therein is in contradiction with the intended object of the injunction.

For in that case, the intended meaning, persisting with stability because it was previously introduced, sets aside the negation— by virtue of the negation’s underlying purpose being to negate what is contrary to itself— and thereby becomes a subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*) for the sake of expressing its own specific qualities.

Therefore, when there is a semblance of negation rather than actual negation, in order to express a particularity of the desired object according to the manner just described, this ornament called *ākṣepa* (the "paralipsis"), which involves a slight possibility of the negation of the intended meaning, is designated by true poets.
The connection is that "the wise are tranquil.
To demonstrate its two-fold division, he says:
"And that [wisdom] is held to be of two kinds, having as its objects that which is yet to be spoken and that which has already been spoken."
The meaning is that *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is of two kinds, because it consists in the statement of a prohibition based on what is intended, whether already stated or yet to be stated.
Now, it was stated that the definition of *ākṣepa* is "like a prohibition of something intended.
And being "intended" (*iṣṭatva*) is the state of being the object of desire (*icchākarmatā*).
Furthermore, an object that is the goal of the act of desiring (*icchā-karma*) does not necessarily become the object of the act of speaking (*ukti-kriyā*).
For that which is desired is sometimes spoken of and sometimes not.

Therefore, raising the objection that the twofold division of implication (*ākṣepa*)—to be described later—as having the "spoken" (*ukta*) as its scope is untenable based on the premise that the desired is the object of speech, he says:
The binding of that [object] and of the thing to be enjoined is said to occur through negation alone.

The "objection" (*ākṣepa*)—referring to the subject matter about to be stated or already stated—is formulated by means of what appears to be a negation of that which is intended to be enjoined or made known. This is what is meant: here, the status of being desired is determined precisely through the medium of being the object of an injunction, because there is no other basis for it.
And "being the object of the act of injunction" (vidhānakarmatā) is the state of being the object of an utterance whose nature is injunctive;
and that is twofold: objective (ārthī) and verbal (śābdī).
Where the intended meaning is understood even without the operation of its own word, but solely by way of negating the operation of other words, there it is "implied" (ārthī).
And in that case, the "suggestion" (ākṣepa) pertains to the subject matter to be stated hereafter.
However, where the intended meaning is expressed directly through the operation of its own word, there it is "verbal" (śābdī).
And in that case, the scope of the *ākṣepa* (poetic suggestion) is that which has been stated.

Thus, according to the principle just explained, when something is intended as the conclusion through an expressed or implied injunction (*vidhi*), it is possible for it to be the object of the act of stating; therefore, the *ākṣepa* is established as having both a "stated scope" (*uktaviṣayatva*) and a "scope to be stated" (*vakṣyamāṇaviṣayatva*), based on that meaning which serves as the object of the act of stating.
In this regard, an example of the objection (*ākṣepa*) concerning a subject that is about to be discussed is as follows:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of Smara, that even in Rudra such a state exists!
Let this matter rest; as for measuring the waters of the ocean with jars, who are we? (Udbhaṭa, *Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha* 2.1)
"Aho" expresses wonder.

Here, it was intended to demonstrate the greatness of Manmatha through contact with that particular state [of passion]; however, that demonstration of his power in such a manner has been prohibited by the words "let this much suffice," and so forth.
And here, the negation follows from the contradiction with being denotable;
for he states the contradiction with being denotable because it is impossible to express such a thing due to its infinity.
Indeed, by stating that even Rudra is in such a state, the greatness of Manmatha is established through a general form, rather than a specific one.
Therefore, this is a prohibition of the description of the particular states of Smara’s greatness intended to be expressed, due to their infinity;
it is not, however, an absolute negation, because it constitutes a subordinate sentence-meaning that would contradict the intended primary meaning.
For instance, in this case, the impossibility of measuring the waters of the ocean with jars— which was stated by us as the subject matter—
is intended to be used for the purpose of exalting, by way of similarity, the specific states of the greatness of the God of Love (Manmatha) characterized by infinity; thus, these states,
being what was previously desired to be communicated and having thereby attained their established status, constitute the meaning of the sentence.
Consequently, because it contradicts that [prohibition], the negation of its expression constitutes a subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*) here.
Yet, a subordinate sentence-meaning cannot be said to be the point of final rest for the sentence.

Indeed, in the case of "the cloth becomes red" (*raktaḥ paṭo bhavati*), since the sentence is directed toward the becoming of the cloth as delimited by redness, it is not well-said to claim that the sentence terminates merely in the becoming of the cloth.

Therefore, here too, since the negation constitutes a subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*), it lacks the status of being the point where the sentence comes to rest; thus, while it has the *appearance* of being a negation, it does not possess the nature of a negation [in the primary sense].

And that negation, functioning here as a subordinate sentence-meaning in accordance with the primary sentence-meaning, explicitly prohibits the specific states of the power of the God of Love (*manmatha*), rather than merely those which are to be understood through the force of the context (*arthasāmarthya*).
And thus, the impossibility of drinking the waters of the ocean with jars—an impossibility performed by us for our own sake—is stated directly by the speaker himself.

When the sentence is understood through that similarity to terminate in a specific quality characterized by the infinity of the particular states of the greatness of Smara (Cupid)—a state devoid of a conventional term—the sentence establishes this desired meaning within that specific quality under the guise of a prohibition; therefore, it is *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis).

And here, by means of the operation of the word "aho" (oh! in the phrase "Oh, the majesty of Smara, that even in Rudra such a state exists!", and through the negation "let this much suffice," there is an indication—by way of being about to be described—of the specific states of the majesty of Love (Manmatha) which, though not explicitly mentioned by the poet's own voice, are nonetheless implied.
And of those [states] thus indicated, there is, under the guise of negation, the presentation of their infinite varieties, which are devoid of a single comprehensive term.

Therefore, the scope of the objection will be stated hereafter; however, as for the example of that [objection] whose scope has already been mentioned: "While he was reflecting, 'How strange that his reflection did not cease,'" [the verse continues: "he saw a woman, beautiful in every limb, standing at the threshold of the palace. This is the example. Thus ends the section on the objection. Now, the example of the "implied" (ākṣepa) is as follows: "As he was thinking, 'How strange that the limit of his thought did not cease,' he saw a woman, beautiful in every limb, standing at the threshold of the palace. This is the example of the implied. Thus ends the section on the implied. Now, the example of the "doubtful" (saṃdeha) is as follows: "Is this a lotus with bees? Or is it a face with eyes? This is the example of the doubtful. Thus ends the section on the doubtful. Now, the example of the "corroboration" (ullekha) is as follows: "The moon, the sun, and fire—these three have become one in you, O fair-faced one. This is the example of the corroboration. Thus ends the section on the corroboration. Now, the example of the "poetic fancy" (bhrāntimān) is as follows: "This is a lotus, surely, because it possesses fragrance and beauty; otherwise, how could there be such a thing? This is the example of the poetic fancy. Thus ends the section on the poetic fancy. Now, the example of the "denial" (apahnuti) is as follows: "This is not the moon; it is a lotus. Nor are these two eyes; they are bees. This is the example of the denial. Thus ends the section on the denial. Now, the example of the "self-disparagement" (svabhāvokti) is as follows: "The lotus, though possessing fragrance and beauty, is devoid of luster; the moon, though possessing luster, is devoid of fragrance and beauty. This is the example of the self-disparagement. Thus ends the section on the self-disparagement. Now, the example of the "exemplification" (nidarśanā) is as follows: "The lotus, having abandoned its own nature, has become like the moon; the moon, having abandoned its own nature, has become like the lotus. This is the example of the exemplification. Thus ends the section on the exemplification. Now, the example of the "concealment" (vyājokti) is as follows: "O friend, do not speak thus; this is not the moon, but a lotus; nor are these two eyes, but bees. This is the example of the concealment. Thus ends the section on the concealment. Now, the example of the "hyperbole" (atiśayokti) is as follows: "The moon has become the lotus; the lotus has become the moon. This is the example of the hyperbole. Thus ends the section on the hyperbole. Now, the example of the "simile" (upamā) is as follows: "Her face is like the moon; her eyes are like lotuses. This is the example of the simile. Thus ends the section on the simile. Now, the example of the "metaphor" (rūpaka) is as follows: "The moon-face; the lotus-eyes. This is the example of the metaphor. Thus ends the section on the metaphor. Now, the example of the "poetic identification" (sāmānyālaṅkāra) is as follows: "The moon is the lotus; the lotus is the moon. This is the example of the poetic identification. Thus ends the section on the poetic identification. Now, the example of the "poetic cause" (hetu) is as follows: "Because of her beauty, she is like the moon; because of her fragrance, she is like the lotus. This is the example of the poetic cause. Thus ends the section on the poetic cause. Now, the example of the "poetic figure of speech" (alaṅkāra) is as follows: "The moon is the lotus; the lotus is the moon. Or where has the end of conceptual constructions of desire, as well as of time, ever been seen?
Here, the statement regarding the "variety" (citratva) that was previously mentioned is challenged by the question "Where [is it]? because it is well-known;
for while in the previous case contradiction (*viruddhatva*) was stated as the basis for the challenge, here it is its being well-known (*prasiddhatva*).
And the objection occurs in only two ways: by way of contradiction and by way of being already established.

As it has been said: “When one speaks of something as an ‘established fact’ or as ‘contradictory,’ having thereby set aside [the opponent’s] statement, and then asserts something else for the sake of establishing that very state, that is an objection (ākṣepa).”
And here, in order to establish its well-known nature, the similarity to time is stated:
just as no end of time is perceived, so it is with the conceptual constructions of desire.
Therefore, there is no violation of the rule here.
Because this form is observed elsewhere as well.
Furthermore, due to the equality of time, the distinction here—consisting in the infinity of conceptualizations of desire—is intended to be devoid of a term for cognition (*saṃvijñāna-pada-śūnya*).

And because that [distinction], which was previously introduced in a general way through its diversity, now constitutes the meaning of the sentence by means of the intended form—which is devoid of a term for cognition and functions as a negation—the negation possesses the status of a subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntara-vākyārthatā*), just as before.
Therefore, this [statement] beginning with "kvaca" is like a negation, but it is not a negation per se;
by that, the scope of the implied objection (ākṣepa) is stated here. As they say:
Alternatively, when an object that is either explicitly mentioned or intended to be spoken is negated,
and its constituent part is negated by way of contradiction with it— where such a negation occurs, that is [the figure of] Akṣepa (Paralipsis).
Thus,
when a word is touched upon— that is,
when it is intended to be spoken— there is an implication regarding the subject matter already mentioned.
However, in the case of the subject matter to be discussed hereafter, that which is intended [as the primary meaning] is the implied sense (ārtha),
because it is presented by way of negating the assistance provided by the operation of other words.

The negation that is performed here in both cases, by virtue of contradicting the intended meaning, abandons its own primary purpose and, by establishing the very intended meaning, becomes subordinate to it.
Therefore, the meaning is that there are two kinds of *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) here.
This is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).

That which occurs before a statement by a capable person, or after that of another, or which occurs in reverse order, or with the utterance of the word "hi," or otherwise; [that is a *vākyaśeṣa*]. (UK 2.4)

That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a corroborative instance). Where there exists a relationship between a probandum (*samarthya*) and its proof (*samarthaka*), that is *arthāntaranyāsa*.

For in that case, without explicitly stating the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—which are the grounds for understanding how the corroborative instance functions as a proof—the presentation is made as if it were another distinct matter.
Because pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), though not explicitly stated by their own names, are implicitly included;
therefore, this is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact).
And that is of four kinds.

In that regard, when the corroborator (*samarthaka*) has been stated first, there are two ways in which the corroboration (*samarthya*) is subsequently expressed. One way is for the relationship between the corroboration and the corroborator to be manifested by the word *hi*. As it has been said: "When the statement of the corroborator comes first, and that of the other [the corroborated] follows."
Thus [it is said], and also: "by the utterance of the word 'for' (*hi*).
An example of this is:
"There is nothing that the world will not do when it has a task at hand."
This Lord Śarva himself was dwelling there, having assumed the form of a young brahmin student.
"Having become a *baṭu*," that is, having attained the state of one who has recently undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Here, having raised the doubt that it is inconsistent for Śarva—who surpasses all the worlds—to adopt the conduct of a *baṭu*, the supporting argument was previously set forth to justify it: "There is nothing he does not do.
Because he is utterly intent on his purpose, he experienced even a form that is improper.
"Śarva is likewise other than such a person.
And here, the relationship between the supported (samarthya) and the support (samarthaka) is manifested by the word *hi*.

Where the supported and the support are presented in the same sequence as before, the word *hi* is not employed because its meaning is understood through the power of the context; there, it is the second variety of *arthāntaranyāsa*.
It occurs;
thus it is said, "and otherwise as well," which means even without the expression of the word "hi" (for/indeed).
An example of this is as follows:
"A concealed mode of conduct is recommended for women when examining their true disposition; therefore, Dhūrjaṭi set out, having assumed the form of a young cowherd boy. (Udbhaṭa-śataka 2.4)
"Bhāva" means intention (*āśaya*). "Bāṭavī" refers to that which pertains to a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Here, the conduct [of Śiva] is praised as being concealed by assuming the guise of a religious student, as expressed in the passage beginning with "the conduct of Dhūrjaṭi... and so forth.
Because he was intent on examining the disposition of a woman, Dhūrjaṭi resorted to a concealed mode of conduct;
for the word *hi* (for) has not been explicitly employed here, as its meaning—"since"—is already understood through the force of the word *ataḥ* (therefore).
Thus, these two instances of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), preceded by a supporting statement (*samarthaka*), have been described.

Even in cases where, by way of reversal, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) is presented first and the corroborative argument (*samarthaka*) afterwards, there too—since the relationship between the capacity and the corroboration is understood through the word *hi* and is implied by the sense—the two-fold division remains.
As it has been said: "Or that which occurs in reverse order, or even otherwise by the utterance of the word *hi*."
An example of the former [direct perception] is as follows: "Then Hara, having established his self by means of the self, entered into meditation;
for that which is meditated upon through meditation does not contradict direct perception."

In this context, since Hara’s [perception] has as its object things that are spatially remote and so forth, his external sensory functions are unimpeded; thus, given the possibility of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) produced by the external senses, it might be considered inappropriate for him to resort to meditation (*dhyāna*).
To justify that [resort to meditation], it is said: "For direct perception would be inconsistent," and so on. [The meaning is:
Hara resorted to meditation because he sought a means of apprehension that is absolutely non-contradictory.
However, where the relationship between the capacity and the possessor of capacity is not explicitly manifested by the word *hi*, but rather the capacity is presented first, that is the example:
"And he saw Umā performing most painful austerities;
for what other recourse is there for maidens who have no desire for a husband? (UK 2.6)

Anticipating the objection—"Since there exist many means for obtaining one's desired boon, such as prayer and the like, why did the Goddess weary her body with asceticism?"—the following was stated to justify it: "Of those who desire an improbable husband.
Because she longed for a husband so difficult to attain, she resorted to asceticism;
for ascetic practices cause weariness even to the Goddess.

Furthermore, she acquires those very things of such a kind; therefore, she performs penance (*tapas*). Since penance is the object of the act of performing penance, there is the grammatical treatment of the agent as the object (*karmavadbhāva*).
In this very manner, the fourfold *arthāntaranyāsa* has been explained.
Now, if *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a corroborative instance) occurs only when there is a relationship between the supported and the support,

then it would follow that *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) and *dṛṣṭānta* (simile) would also be instances of *arthāntaranyāsa*, since the relationship between the supported and the support exists in them as well.
To explain:

"Behold the fruit of the trees, which is pleasing to those who love it, sweet, and ripened in due time, [obtained] without human effort. In this instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), there is the comprehension of a general principle from a particular case; namely, that the various qualities possessed by the forest trees [arise] without human activity such as watering and so forth.
"The production of fruit is primarily dependent on destiny; thus, everything in this world is primarily dependent on destiny.
Herein, there exists a relationship between the probans and the probandum:
all activity in the world is primarily dependent on destiny because it does not conform to the presence or absence of human effort, just like the fruit of forest trees.
Furthermore,
since that too would result in the undesirable consequence of being an *arthāntaranyāsa*, the definition suffers from the flaw of over-extension (*alakṣyavyāpti*).
Moreover, this applies even to the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) [once it has been established].
A relationship of capacity exists;
for it is said: "The moment you are seen, her mind, ignited by the god of love, is extinguished;
for at the light of the moon, the night-lily of the night-lily-pond blossoms."
In this regard, just as the night-lotus (*kumuda*) blooms at the sight of the moon because the night-lotus bed is partial to the qualities of the moon,

so too, due to its partiality for your virtues, may your mind— though ignited by the fire of love— be pacified upon seeing you. Anticipating the objection that, because of this relationship between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would also result in being a *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), he says:
Because it establishes the matter at hand,
it stands distinct from both the praise of something irrelevant (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) and in the *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), the relationship between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*) is indeed perceived;
however, in those cases, the possibility of such a relationship does not exist in the same way as it does in *arthāntaranyāsa*.
For in *arthāntaranyāsa*, the support of the subject to be supported occurs through its own explicit mention, occurring either before or after [the general proposition], as appropriate.
In Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), the subject at hand is implied by the power of the non-contextual matter, but it is not explicitly stated by its own name,
as in the example previously described.

For in that case, by means of the sight of fruit on forest trees—which is irrelevant and emphasizes destiny—the primacy of destiny, which pertains to the entire world, is implied as the relevant subject; however, it is not explicitly stated by its own name as it is in the figure *arthāntaranyāsa*.

Consequently, even though a relationship between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*) exists there, because it does not reside in the relevant subject introduced by the words, it does not possess the nature of *arthāntaranyāsa*.

Furthermore, in the case of a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example), since both the corroborator (*samarthaka*) and the corroborated (*samarthya*) are explicitly stated by their own words, even though it possesses the quality of being based on the subject matter (*prakṛtārtha*) expressed through its own words, it does not constitute *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact).
This is because the *dṛṣṭānta* functions by placing the relationship between the corroborator and the corroborated at the forefront;
indeed, its operation does not proceed by placing that relationship at the forefront.
Because the mere relationship between an object and its reflection is not touched upon by the word;
for in that case, the determination of the relationship between the capable and the capable-of-being-capacitated (*samartha-samarthaka-bhāva*) arises from the sense (*artha*).
In the figure of *arthāntaranyāsa*, however, the introduction is made precisely through the relationship between the capable and the capable-of-being-capacitated.

Therefore, where there is the introduction of another matter based on the relationship between the capable (samartha) and the capable-to-be (samarthya), it does not follow that the example (dṛṣṭānta) becomes a case of *arthāntaranyāsa*, because it is already [included] within that category. This is what is meant by the phrase "for the purpose of supporting the subject matter at hand" (*prakṛtārthasamarthanāt*). In this context, the word "subject matter at hand" (*prakṛta*) should be understood as referring specifically to the subject matter explicitly mentioned by its own name.
And here, "establishment" (samarthana) is understood as that which occurs in the state of the commencement [of the argument].
Vyatireka (Distinction):
That which consists in the specific mention of a quality belonging to either the standard of comparison (upamāna) or the object of comparison (upameya),
based on whether the cause [of that quality] is perceived or not perceived, is of two kinds.
Where the distinction between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is made manifest, that is *vyatireka* (distinction).

For in that case, there is an "excess" (*ati-rikta*), meaning a superiority, of the subject of comparison over the object of comparison, or of the object of comparison over the subject of comparison, by virtue of some particular quality; therefore, it is called *vyatireka*.
And it is of two kinds.
In this regard, there is one variety [of suggestion] due to the implication (ākṣepa) of the cause for the manifestation of a distinction through the force of the meaning;
another, however, is due to its being expressed by its own word.
As it has been said: "It is twofold, according to whether the cause is not seen or is seen."
Moreover, each of these two varieties is itself twofold:

in some cases, when the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is understood through the power of the sense, the *vyatireka* (distinction) is expressed by means of the two aforementioned modes; in other cases, however, it is conveyed by the use of words such as *iva*.

In that regard, where the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is understood through the power of the sense, there is the first variety among the two preceding types; an example of this is as follows:
"Having gone to the peak of Gaurī, she beheld Umā, emaciated by her ascetic penance, from afar, her body surpassing the form of the moon whose luster had been swallowed by Rāhu. (Uttarakāṇḍa 2.7)

"By whom the light has been made internal, like the swallowing by Rāhu of a liquid substance such as water, which consists of its being contained within the cavity of his own throat"— thus it is said. Here, the body of the moon, characterized by its light having been swallowed by Rāhu, is the object of comparison.
Pārvatī, emaciated by asceticism, is the object of comparison;
the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of these two is a lack of luster due to external causes, even though natural beauty exists.
And that [attribute], although not explicitly stated by the author himself, is obtained through a consideration of the nature of the things themselves.

Thus, even in the absence of words such as "iva," the cognition of the relationship between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) arises here by virtue of contextual implication; and in this way, the distinction of the object of comparison from the standard of comparison is made known.
Furthermore, the cause for that being-expressed distinction is not explicitly stated by its own throat [i.e., directly], but rather it is understood through the force of the meaning (arthasāmarthya).

Rāhu is not capable of drinking the radiance of the moon in the same way that Pārvatī is capable of emaciating herself through the excellence of her asceticism; thus, here the excellence of the subject (the object of comparison) over the standard of comparison (Rāhu) is understood from the very excellence of her penance as the cause of distinction. This is therefore *vyatireka* (distinction) with an unstated cause.
As for *vyatireka* with a stated cause—
She constantly surpassed with her face, which possessed a shimmering luster, the lotus that is devoid of beauty at night and the moon that lacks radiance by day.
The face is the object of comparison (upameya),
while the lotus and the moon are the standards of comparison (upamāna);
and here, both of these are touched by one's own throat.

In these two cases, however, their common property—such as loveliness—and the relationship between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) are both understood through the force of the context.

Indeed, unlike the vyatireka (distinction) to be described later, particles such as *iva*, which indicate the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison, have not been employed here.
Furthermore, by the phrase "making [the moon] inferior," the superiority of the object of comparison over the standard of comparison is made manifest.
And therein, the *nimitta* (the cause or ground) is employed as the substratum for both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*).

Regarding the two objects of comparison—the lotus and the moon—their lack of beauty and lack of luster respectively at night and during the day are the grounds; whereas in the case of the objects compared, their radiance shines throughout both night and day.
Therefore, this is a case of *vyatireka* (dissimilation) based on the perception of a distinction [between the two].

Thus, in cases where the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is not indicated by particles such as *iva*, the two types of *vyatireka* have been shown.
However, regarding the *vyatireka* that occurs when the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* is expressed by means of *iva* and so forth, he says:
That which is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), endowed with "just as" (yathā) and so forth,
is also accepted here as a negative concomitance (vyatireka), because it involves the application of a specific qualification.

The definition of the negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) has been applied through the phrases "the example by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa dṛṣṭānta*) and "because of the connection with the production of a distinction" (*viśeṣāpādanānvayāt*).
For dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is indeed the absence of the property of the object of comparison (*upameya*) in the object of comparison (*upamāna*).

By the phrase "endowed with *yathā*, *iva*, and so forth," he states that the relationship between the object of comparison and the object of similarity is indicated by *yathā*, *iva*, and other such particles.
An illustration of this is as follows:
"Though she remained engaged in austerities that were difficult even for those who subsist on withered leaves, water, and air,
she did not display any extraordinary pride like other ascetics."
The consumption of withered leaves, water, and wind constitutes the austerity;
here, other ascetics are the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), while the Blessed One is the subject of comparison (*upameya*).

And the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is the mind’s state of exhilaration resulting from being established in arduous austerity. Furthermore, the suffix *vat* here serves as the basis for conveying the relationship of similarity (*upamānopameyabhāva*), since that exhilaration of the mind is the very ground upon which [the comparison] rests. By stating "not bearing pride" (*garvaṃ na samudvahantīm*), the distinction of the object of comparison (*upameya*) from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is expressed.
It is said that other ascetics, their minds becoming agitated through the power of excessive austerity, harbor pride;
but the Blessed Lady, because her mind is utterly tranquil, does not do so.
Thus, in this case, the similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is based on the state of the onset of pride.
However, because that [likeness] is not fully sustained, there is a distinction (*vyatireka*) of the object of comparison (*upameya*) from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

And regarding this non-sustenance, the cause—though not explicitly stated by its own throat—is understood through the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*), namely, the state of having a mind that is utterly tranquil.
Thus, this has been illustrated as *vyatireka* where the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison is expressed, even though the cause for the distinction is not perceived.
However, when there is the apprehension of a sign (*nimitta*), an example for that should be inferred.
Thus, these four types of exclusion (*vyatireka*) have been explained;
[this refers to] those two exclusions which arise from the perception and non-perception of a sign.

Since each individual relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is twofold— depending on whether terms such as *iva* (like) and so forth are employed or not—
these four types of *vyatireka* (distinction) further yield another four varieties when words suitable for *śliṣṭokti* (paronomasia) are employed. Thus it is said:
When words suitable for double entendre are cited separately,
the resulting production of a distinction is known as Vyatireka (Distinction).

The term *śliṣṭa* (paronomastic) has the definition that will be stated later, beginning with "pronounced by a single effort. When the utterance appropriate for a paronomastic ornament (*śliṣṭālaṅkāra*) is not employed either through *tantra* (simultaneous application) or as the cause for the employment of another similar word, but rather separately,
then, when a distinction is brought about, there occurs *vyatireka* (distinction).
An illustration of this is as follows:

"That wondrous winter splendor, renowned for being achieved in a single month through austerity—[the Goddess] now casts it far below by means of her exceedingly long austerity. (Udbhaṭa, Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha 2.10)
In this instance, the beauty of the cool season is the standard of comparison (upamāna), the Blessed Lady is the object of comparison (upameya),
and their common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma) is the state of being endowed with asceticism (tapoyuktatva).
In one case it is the month of Māgha for ascetic penance,
while in the other it is the performance of difficult austerities as a cause for spiritual advancement.
Particles such as *iva* and others, though not explicitly mentioned here, are understood by implication.
The contrast, however, is that [the other] bestows [merit] from afar, while this [practice] bestows it "downward" (i.e., directly).
And the cause for that is the identity of duration and the length of the two ascetic practices (*tapas*).
And that [distinction] is presented respectively as residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).

In that context, when the relationship of comparison and the object of comparison is not expressed by means of suffixes such as *-vat* and the like, the figure of *vyatireka* (distinction) is illustrated by showing the underlying cause.

In this same manner, when there is a composition of words suitable for "punning" (*śliṣṭokti*), other instances of *vyatireka* should also be cited according to the threefold division previously stated.
Vibhāvanā:
When there is a negation of an action, that which is the manifestation of its result is to be known as vibhāvanā itself, occurring when concentration (samādhi) is easily attained. (UK 2.9)
Whatever is known here, all that is the fruit of action (*kriyāphala*).

Since the arising of an effect from causes occurs by way of action, and because all things that have become effects are perceived in their phenomenal form (*prātītika-rūpa*), action alone is the immediate cause of all fruits. Furthermore, there are cases where action is negated, yet the arising of the fruit of action is still taught.
In that regard, there is an ornament called *vibhāvanā*.
It is described as the arising of an effect even in the absence of its cause;
thus, it is a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or production that appears to be contradictory (*viruddhābhāsā*).
Therefore, there is a refutation [of that objection].

But if this is so, does it not follow that the fault is rendered futile, since it has been stated that "a view whose meaning is contradictory is futile"? To this he says: "when meditative concentration (samādhi) is easily attained.
Here, *samādhi* means the rebuttal (*parihāra*).
The meaning is that where a rebuttal of the contradiction is easily obtained;
an example of such [a case] is as follows:
"Aṅgalekhā, whose body was reddened by the application of saffron..."
And she bore the imprint of a lip, copper-red though unstained with lac.
The "limb-line" (*aṅgalekhā*) refers to the slender body.
*Kāramīra* is saffron.
This yellowish hue of the body, which is observed among heroines upon close inspection, is the effect of the action characterized by the application of saffron unguents.
The yellowish hue on the body of the Blessed Lady was not produced by the application of saffron;
therefore, the teaching here concerns the result—the yellowish hue—which remains even after the cessation of the action characterized by the application of saffron.
And the resolution to this is that such a hue is natural (*svābhāvikatayā*).
Thus, this is *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect arising without its cause).

In the phrase "her eyes, copper-hued though not with lac," the production of redness—the result of the action of applying lac—is indicated as being natural (*svābhāvikī*), despite the negation of that causal action;
therefore, it is *vibhāvanā*.

And here, through hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), one should understand the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of the natural yellowness and so forth, which serves as the object of comparison (*upameya*), with the yellowness and so forth produced by saffron and other substances, which serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
This is *samāsokti*:
"By means of a sentence whose primary sense is the subject at hand, [an implied meaning is suggested] through its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) which are common to both."
The statement of an irrelevant matter is cited as *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis).

Where a sentence is centered on the subject at hand (*prastutārtha*), and through qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that are identical to those used for it, there are other qualifiers belonging to an irrelevant matter (*aprakṛtārtha*) which, by virtue of their similarity, bring to mind that irrelevant matter as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*);
that is *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis), because it expresses two meanings—the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—in a concise manner.
An example of this is as follows:
Her jasmine-like teeth shone with radiance, her hands were as beautiful as young shoots, and she was slender;
having gone to the forest, she resembled a creeper upon which a swarm of bees had settled in the form of her matted locks.

In this context, the teeth’s radiance, the hands, and the matted locks—which serve as epithets of the Blessed Lady—are respectively pervaded by superimpositions (āropa) in the form of creepers, flowers, sprouts, and bees;
thus they attain the nature of those [objects].
Slenderness, however, is a quality common to both the Blessed Lady and the creepers.

And by the word "forest" (*vana*), which serves as the cause for the emergence of a metaphorical suggestion (*rūpakapratibhā*) through the device of paronomasia (*śleṣa*), the water—which is the support for the Blessed Lady’s ascetic practice—is figuratively represented by the grove, which is the support for the creepers.
Therefore, these adjectives are common to both the Blessed Lady, who is the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), and the creeper, which is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*).
By the force of this [similarity], the creeper, being the object of comparison (*upameya*), is implied as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the Blessed Lady, who is the subject at hand.
Therefore, this is *samāsokti* (abridged expression).
As for *atiśayokti* (hyperbole):
when, by reason of some cause, an object transcends the limits of the world.
Therefore, the wise consider that hyperbole to be an ornament.
Where non-difference is perceived despite difference, or where diversity is bound within what is otherwise [unified],
such is the expression of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) in the composition of a matter that is being conceived.
Where, due to a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect,
one clings to the notion of simultaneity, that [person] is also bound as before.
Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is that statement which, relying on some cause, is composed with a scope that transcends the world.
It has four varieties: the first is where there is non-difference or identity (*aikya*) in what is actually different;
the second is where there is difference or diversity (*nānātva*) in what is actually not different or identical.
Likewise, when there is a composition based merely on the possibility of an object that does not exist externally, it is the third variety.

As for cause and effect, because the effect arises so rapidly, there is a reversal of the sequence [of cause preceding effect]; this is the fourth variety. An example of the first variety is as follows:
By the wealth of her own beauty, which vibrated with the splendor of her asceticism,
she was undoubtedly seen as not emaciated at all, even though she was thin.

In this context, although the emaciation produced by asceticism—which arose after the state of emaciation the Blessed Lady previously possessed—was distinct from it, it is described as non-different; thus, she is [described] as "not emaciated.
And the cause for this is that her mass of beauty was rendered extraordinary by the splendor of her asceticism.
Therefore, by virtue of this cause, the scope of this statement transcends the world.
Therefore, this is an instance of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
Now, an example of the second variety [of *atiśayokti*] follows: "And the Blessed One thought: 'Oh, how truly delightful is this!'"
By her asceticism, a transformation has been brought about, which is evident from her transition from childhood and the other stages of life.

Here, although the Blessed Lady remains in the state of maidenhood (*kaumāra*), she is described as being endowed with that stage of youth which occurs subsequent to it; thus, there is a distinction from her maidenhood.
And the cause for this is the loveliness produced by her asceticism (*tapas*).
Therefore, this is an imposition of difference upon what is essentially non-different.

Now, an example of the third variety [of *upamā*]: "If the moonlight of the moon were to fall upon her blooming lotus-like face, then it would be comparable to the rosary of pearl beads in her hand. (UKSS 2.15)
The phrase "a mass of moonlight" refers to the manner of the moon's radiance;
the connection is that this would serve as a simile for the pearl rosary in her hand at that time.

Here, although the blossoming of a lotus upon contact with the rays of the moon is impossible in reality—since its contraction is observed—the poet-creator, through his own activity produced by poetic intuition (*pratibhā*), renders it as something possible.
This has been demonstrated;
therefore, what is presented here is a composition based on a possible meaning.
And the cause for the possibility of that meaning, which transcends the sphere of the world, is the sight of the pearl rosary resting upon the hand of the Blessed Lady.

For instance: first of all, this unprecedented relationship between a support and its supported—namely, the white jasmine flower and the pearl rosary—which transcends the world, has been observed by us.

If a similar relationship of support and supported were to exist between the blooming lotus and the rays of the moon, then a relationship of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva) would arise here; thus, such a possibility is entertained.
Therefore, in this case, because a similar object is perceived, even a thing that is otherwise impossible is described as if it were possible.
Indeed, when one object is perceived, even though another is not observed, there arises the conceptualization of something belonging to that same class;
just as, for example, when a southerner has seen one camel, there arises the conceptualization of other unobserved camels.
Therefore, in this case, the conceptualization is based on a cause.
And by this manner, the absence of any comparison for the subject matter at hand is demonstrated here, [showing] that "there is nothing else whatsoever that can serve as its comparison.
For this very reason, the word *yadi* ("if") is employed with the desire to refute the object that has been presented merely as a possibility.
Indeed, it is the word *yadi* that indicates a doubt (*āśaṅkā*) in this context.
Doubt arises regarding an object whose existence is not yet certain.

And when an object whose existence is uncertain is presented by the creative genius of a poet as having a possible form, its incomparability is perceived for as long as it is not being refuted by worldly cognition— which concerns objects fashioned by the ancient Prajāpati and which is contrary to that [poetic presentation].
Thus is this third variety;
the fourth, however, is as follows:
"I believe her side-long glances fall behind her toward the various directions."
Generally, however, it is the successive volleys of Love’s arrows that go first.
In this context, the casting of side-glances in these directions is the cause,
while the arrival of a succession of Cupid’s arrows is the effect.
Regarding cause and effect, the cause possesses an inherent priority in time, whereas the effect possesses posteriority.

But here, the reverse is the case; because the effect is connected by its prior existence and the cause by its subsequent occurrence, the side-glances fall behind from the front, while the succession of Cupid’s arrows moves ahead. The cause for this is [as follows]: *Note: The Sanskrit term *nimitta* appears at the end of the provided text fragment.*
The effect arises with extreme rapidity;
therefore, this statement, by virtue of that [cause], has a sphere of operation that transcends the world. Consequently, it is a hyperbolic expression (*atiśayokti*).
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Laghuvṛtti* on the *Udbhaṭālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious Great Chamberlain Indurāja.
Now begins the third chapter:
"Enumeration," "Poetic Fancy," and likewise "Natural Description."
Others say there are three ornaments for the adornment of speech.
Regarding "according to order" (yathāsaṃkhyam):
when there are many things taught that do not share the same properties, that sequential restatement [of them] is called "according to order. (UK 3.2)
When, after items have been previously mentioned, other corresponding items are subsequently specified in sequence, there occurs the figure of speech called *yathāsaṃkhya* (enumeration).
For in that case, the connection between the objects—though not explicitly conveyed by words—is relied upon without deviating from the order indicated by their numbering.
Thus, because it suggests the sequential connection of the objects, this figure is termed *yathāsaṃkhya*.

Furthermore, since this ornament, even when applied sparingly to many [objects], becomes bound with beauty, it is said to belong to "many" (*bhūyasām*). For when it is applied to only two [objects], as long as its composition is not performed in a manner characterized by fourfold quality and so forth, it does not possess beauty. However, for many objects, it becomes charming with only a small effort, corresponding to their number.
For in that case, when it is doubled or tripled in its application, an excellence of beauty arises.
As it has been said:
"When many [elements] are indicated, that which is doubled or tripled becomes beautiful."
Therefore, one should follow the very path used for those [other] two, and should apply it to the remaining two in many ways.
Thus [it is said].

Now, in the example to be described later, such as "The lotus-stalk and the swan" (*mṛṇālahaṃsa*), the hearts of connoisseurs are captivated by the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction), which highlights the specific qualities of the subjects—the arms and so forth—over their points of comparison—the lotus-stalks and so forth;
it is not, however, by means of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence).

Anticipating the objection as to how this can be a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) based on numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), it is said: "of things possessing dissimilar properties" (*asadharmaṇām*).

For even in cases where, due to the absence of commonality, there is no relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison—and thus no possibility of employing figures such as *vyatireka* (distinction)—this [correspondence] still brings about an excellence of beauty; this is the meaning.
As, for example:

May Hari, Hara, and the four-faced Brahmā— possessing the luster of collyrium, snow, and gold, and riding upon Garuḍa, the bull, and the swan respectively, and seated upon the ocean, the mountain, and the lotus— grant us prosperity.
Thus [it is said].

For here, among the three subjects mentioned—Hari and the others—the attributes such as being smeared with collyrium, having Garuda as a vehicle, and residing in the ocean are respectively enumerated;
yet there is no mutual similarity among them.
Nevertheless, through a sequential consideration, since a correspondence is perceived among the objects according to their respective order, there exists an excellence of beauty.

Therefore, even though this [figure] lacks similarity (*sādharmya*) and the like, because it attains the status of a distinct ornament (*alaṅkāra*), its character as an ornament is unavoidable even in cases where similarity and so forth are present.

Consequently, in the example beginning with "the lotus-stalk and the swan" (*mṛṇālahaṃsa*), *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) should be seen as a subordinate element of the ornament *vyatireka* (contrast).
Therefore, this is a *saṅkara* (commixture) based on the relationship of primary and subordinate members;
as he will state: "Where figures of speech stand by mutual assistance and do not attain their own existence through independence—that too is *saṅkara*."
Thus,
these should be taught as distinct figures of speech according to their respective order.
An example of this is as follows:
By her arms, her gait, and her face, she clearly surpasses the lotus stalks, swans, and lotuses;
it is evident that she has conquered all lotus ponds.
Here, in relation to the arms, the walk, and the face which have been mentioned, the lotus stalk, the swan, and the lotus are subsequently mentioned in their respective order.

By virtue of this, even though the correspondence was not explicitly stated by the words, it is contained within the meaning; thus, due to the presence of such figurative expression (*vakrabhaṇiti*), there is the figure of speech known as *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence).

Poetic Fancy (utprekṣā)—when the actual nature of similarity is not intended to be expressed, it consists of words containing "iva" and the like; it is endowed with an excellence [of expression] through the attribution of qualities or actions that do not belong to the object itself. (UK 3.3)

Where the connection with words such as *iva* and the like is present, yet the form of similarity (*sāmya*) is not intended to be expressed, there is the poetic figure known as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Now, one might object: "If this were so, the flaw of definition known as 'impossibility' (*asambhava*) would follow; for if the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*)—which is what is illuminated—is absent, it would follow that words such as *iva* could not be employed. Anticipating this objection, it is stated: "Because of the lack of connection with those qualities and actions" (*atadguṇakriyāyogāt*).
A quality (*guṇa*) is an established property of a substance (*dravyadharma*),
whereas an action (*kriyā*) has a nature that is yet to be accomplished;
indeed, this entire universe [is thus constituted].
It is twofold because its nature consists of both independent (*svatantra*) and dependent (*paratantra*) categories.
That which is an independent category is designated as the *dharmin* (the subject).
And this is a substance (*dravya*), because it is capable of being referred to by all pronouns, such as "this" or "that."
The dependent nature of an entity consists in its character as a phenomenon (dharma),
and it is twofold,
distinguished by the difference between that which is established and that which is to be established.
In this regard, that which is established as a property (*dharma*) is a quality (*guṇa*),
whereas that which is yet to be accomplished is an action (*kriyā*);
and these are all the worldly categories of entities (*padārtha*).
Because universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are included within this very form of cognition;

for when there is a desire not to express similarity—due to the connection with those actions and qualities of the subject at hand (the *prakṛta*) which possess the characteristics just mentioned—the employment of words such as *iva* is established even in the absence of such an intention.

Indeed, where there is similarity by way of the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), there arises in the subject of comparison a cognition of the actions and qualities residing in the object of comparison, owing to its resemblance to that object.

Furthermore, even in the case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), those actions and qualities belonging to that non-contextual object—which is not explicitly indicated as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—are nevertheless attributed to the contextual object. Therefore, because of this connection with qualities and actions not [inherently] belonging to it, terms such as *iva* (like) and so forth must be expressed.
