For this very reason, this is called poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) because it consists in the "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) of attributes belonging to one thing which have been detached from their own substratum and, by being superimposed upon another object, have attained excellence through their suitability for manifesting rasa and bhāva.
One might object: "Even so, this is even more impossible;

for it is not possible to attribute the qualities of one thing to another thing. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "endowed with excellence. The meaning is that by means of a transformation of form bestowed by the ancient Prajāpati, the poet-creator, desiring to express an excellence of quality in an object, is able to attribute even another form to it.

And this *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is a probability (*saṃbhāvanā*) whose object transcends the world, consisting in the description of an entity that is impossible in the external world as if it were possible.
It is of two kinds, because what is being described— whether it be an existent (*bhāva*) or a non-existent (*abhāva*)— is something impossible in the external world.
Thus it is said:
"This poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is a creative conception whose object transcends the world, arising from the conceit of existence and non-existence."

The meaning is that this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), which has as its object a realm transcending the world, possesses a twofold nature due to the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding either existence or non-existence. Now, if it is said that poetic fancy occurs when there is the employment of words such as *iva* and so forth, then [consider the following]: "Intoxicated by the wind from the breath of serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees..."
In spring, this Malaya breeze causes travelers to swoon.

Fearing that, as in such cases, the absence of the employment of words like "iva" would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of there being no poetic fancy (utprekṣā), he says: "It is expressed by means of words such as 'iva'. (UK 3.4)
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is indeed twofold:

one occurs when words such as "as if" (iva) and so forth are employed; the other occurs even when words such as "as if" are not employed, being understood through the force of the sense (arthasāmarthya).
In this regard, that which is to be expressed by words such as *iva* (like) and so forth through their own explicit mention is expressed by those very words;
however, where it is understood through *iva* and so forth implied by the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*), there is no employment of *iva* and the like.

And in examples such as "the Malaya breeze with serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees," the fact that the Malaya breeze is the cause of the fainting of travelers—due to its being the basis for the manifestation of the god of love—is [understood through implication].

In that context, when the state of being fainting from the serpent's breath is being poetically imagined (utprekṣyamāṇa) as the cause, the sense of "as if" (iva) and so forth is understood through the power of the meaning itself;
therefore, words such as *iva* are not employed.
This is because words like *iva* are used only when the poetic imagination is to be determined by the power of the word *iva* itself.

In that regard, an example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) proceeding from the superimposition of a connection with qualities due to the conceit of existence is as follows: "By her prayers, which were like the sunlight drunk by her gaze fixed upon the orb of the sun at all times, a dark spot has fallen upon her face, as if from the delusion that it was the moon. (UK 3.2)
The connection is that [the moon] has fallen with a dark mark due to the *japa* (repetitions) being the cause;
here, the Goddess, intent on her *japa*, looked toward the sun, and thus a dark spot arose upon her face which resembles the moon.
And here, the birth of that dark spot is represented by means of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) as having the form of a "falling" (i.e., it has fallen).
And here, that dark spot (*śyāmikā*) is equal to the hare (*śaśa*) which is the mark of the moon (*śaśilāñchana*).

Therefore, because of its equality with the hare that marks the moon, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in which the subordinate object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the subject of comparison (*upameya*), expressed as "the dark spot itself is the mark.
And regarding that mark, which is colored by darkness, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is conceived that it is the moon, on account of its falling upon the face of the Blessed Lady.

This mark of the moon, which takes the form of a dark spot, has fallen upon the face of the Blessed Lady due to a mere delusion of it being the moon; and this delusion of it being the moon is a quality (*guṇa*),
because, while possessing the nature of an established entity, it is a property of a substance (*dravyadharma*).
And thus, here a dark spot resembling a hare does not perceive the face of the Blessed Lady as the moon because it is devoid of consciousness.
Nevertheless, a connection is established for that [spot]—which has been made into a hare—with the conscious attribute characterized by the delusion of being the moon.
Therefore, in this case, the application of words such as "moon" proceeds from the association with that quality of the other entity (the conscious one), which is characterized by delusion.

The whirling of the moon is a quality (*guṇa*) consisting of an actual state (*bhāva*), which has been superimposed (*adhyavasita*) by the Blessed Lord through the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the speaker fashioned by the poet, because it is the agent of making the darkness [of night] appear like a hare-mark.
Therefore, this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the conceit of an actual state through its connection with a quality that it does not actually possess.
In the same way, whatever poetic fancy arises from the superimposition of a connection with an action (*kriyā*) through the conceit of an actual state, that should be cited as an example of it.
Now, as an example of that [superimposition] which proceeds by superimposing an action upon an object that is non-existent:
"Alas! Her two cheek-plates, having become so [emaciated], have reached such a state of thinness that they seem, as it were, unable to see one another. (Uttararāmacarita 3.3)

Here, the mutual non-perception of the two cheek-plates, which have become emaciated due to the power of asceticism, is of the nature of an absence; because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*) as the cause for the emaciation, which is of the nature of an action.

Thus, this is an *utprekṣā* based on the attribution of an absence due to the connection with a non-existent action. In the same way, one should provide examples for that *utprekṣā* which consists in the attribution of an absence through the connection with the non-possession of a quality (*atadguṇa*).
Svabhāvokti (Description of Nature): The depiction of the gestures of someone engaged in an action—such as a young deer or similar being—is cited as Svabhāvokti. (UK 3.5)

*Śvabhāvokti* (Description of Nature) is the depiction of those specific manifestations of intent—such as the gestures of a young bird and the like—which arise when it is engaged in an activity appropriate to itself, according to its own species.
Its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) arises from its power to suggest (*dhvani*) the essential nature of a unique object.
An example of it is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions]
Having vanished for a moment, then turning halfway with its horn, and pushing ahead for a moment—
this young deer makes me tremble with affection.
They will perish;
for, because the elision of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa) is optional according to the rule "ajāntanaśāṃ vibhāṣā," its non-application occurs here.

In this regard, [the Lord] is being overwhelmed by an intense flow of compassion, like a mother toward her young fawn, as he causes the Blessed One—who is naturally affectionate—to be agitated by a heart overflowing with pity.
Its nature consists of being bound for a moment, remaining invisible, turning over with half its body, and pushing with its horn, and so forth.
Thus ends the third section in this brief commentary on the *Udbhaṭālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha* composed by the illustrious Great Chamberlain Indurāja.
Now begins the fourth section:
*Preyaḥ*, *Rasavat*, *Ūrjasvi*, *Paryāyokta*, and *Samāhita*.
Others know that there are two types of *udātta* (the sublime) as well as *śliṣṭa* (the paronomastic), which constitute poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
The suffix *matup* is applied to the whole [compound] as in *preyasvat*.
Regarding "śliṣṭa" (coalesced):
the meaning is that, just like the high-pitched (*udātta*), *śliṣṭa* is likewise of two kinds.
Furthermore, the twofold nature of the *śliṣṭa* (pun) is stated here for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions.
For Bhāmaha states that the *śliṣṭa* is threefold, saying: "It is of three kinds according to the indication of its co-utterance (*sahokti*), comparison (*upamā*), or cause (*hetu*).
Therefore, it was said "thus" (*tathā*) in order to dispel such misconceptions.
The statement "but the acute [vowel] is of two kinds" is a restatement (anuvāda) for the sake of providing an illustration;

the meaning is that just as the twofold nature of the acute vowel is accepted because it is established by valid means of knowledge, so too should that [twofold nature] be accepted for the *śliṣṭa* [vowel].
First, regarding *preyasvat* (the "affectionate" or "lovely"):
that poetry which is composed by the wise, indicating emotions such as love (*rati*) and others through their consequents (*anubhāva*) and so forth, is called *preyasvat*. (UK 4.2)
The emotional states (*bhāva*) are of three kinds: the stable (*sthāyin*), the transitory (*vyabhicārin*), and the involuntary (*sāttvika*).
Among these, it is proclaimed that "love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder, are the stable emotional states."
Disgust, lack of confidence, envy, intoxication,
fatigue, as well as laziness, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude;
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness,
pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy.
Awakening from sleep, indignation, dissimulation,
and ferocity; intelligence, disease, madness, and likewise death.
Terror and deliberation are also to be known as transitory states;
these thirty-three are the emotional states (bhāvas).
“Stupefaction, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling,
change of color, tears, and fainting— these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions].”
The indicators of these fifty states are fourfold:
the consequent emotion (*anubhāva*), the determinant emotion (*vibhāva*), the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārī*), and the word itself (*svaśabda*).
Among these, the consequent emotion (*anubhāva*) is of four kinds.
It is fourfold: physical (āṅgika), vocal (vācika), internal (sāttvika), and extraneous (āhārya).
The physical consists of the gestures of the hands and so forth;
the vocal consists of the employment of modulations of voice and the like.
The sattvic [anubhāvas] are paralysis and so forth;
the artificial (āhārya), however, are masks, costumes, and the like.
Thus, this fourfold category of anubhāvas, being effects, makes known the bhāvas that serve as their causes.
The determinants (vibhāva), however, are of two kinds,
because they consist of the objective basis (ālambana) and the excitant (uddīpana).
Among these, the objective determinant (ālambana-vibhāva) is that upon which the arising of love and other emotions depends.
For example, Sītā and others [are the excitants] for Rāma and others.

The excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), however, is that by virtue of which there occurs an intense illumination of states such as love (*rati*); for example, the season, garlands, ointments, and so forth.
Thus, this twofold *vibhāva* is the cause of [emotions] such as love (*rati*). And because it is the cause, it makes known the effects, such as love,
just as the rising of very dense dark clouds indicates rain.

For just as a well-discriminated effect is invariably concomitant with its cause, so too a well-discriminated cause is frequently seen in worldly practice to be invariably concomitant with its effect;
therefore, the *vibhāva*, being a cause, makes known the *rasas* such as love (*rati*) which are its effects.
The *vyabhicārin*, however, consists of specific states such as despondency (*nirveda*) and the like, which take the form of particular conditions of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love.
And that [transitory state], such as despondency (nirveda) and so forth, is a specific condition of the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) because it coexists with them;
and because of this coexistence, it brings the stable emotions to their full manifestation, just as one wheel of a chariot causes the other wheel to turn.
However, the term for the emotion itself refers to love (rati) and the like.
And that [suggestion] makes the states (bhāvas) understood by virtue of being expressive.

Although it is not observed that words such as "love" (*rati*) and so forth serve as the basis for the cognition of love and the like— which possess a specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) that is the exclusive domain of the consequents (*anubhāva*)—
nevertheless, they do indeed exist, even if only partially, as the basis for the cognition of love and the like, just like the consequents themselves.

Just as powers (*anubhāva*) and the like do not make things known by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather by way of their general form (*sāmānyarūpa*), so too it should be understood for words themselves; let this suffice.
Thus, these four are the causes for the comprehension of entities (*bhāva*).
As Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa has said: "Entities possess four forms."

Thus, when a poem is composed by means of the indications— whether collectively or individually as appropriate— of these fifty states such as love (*rati*) and the rest, through their fourfold manifestations (*anubhāva*) and so forth; and when these states, which possess their own specific characteristics and have been brought into a general condition, are fully set forth, that poem is called *preyasvat* (possessing the lovely).
By means of the *vibhāva*—the object of aesthetic relish (*ratyālambana*) which is more dear than anything else and denoted by the word *preyas*—*rati* (love) is indicated.
And through its association with that [love], the fifty *bhāvas*, beginning with love, are understood.
Thus, the designation "possessing the *preyas*" (*preyasvat*) is applied to *bhāva-kāvya* (poetry of emotion) by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And here, the figures of speech are the ornaments, while the poem is that which is to be ornamented.
An example of this is as follows:
Out of affection for her son, she felt no difference between him and her own child; full of longing, she began to fondle him, taking him onto her lap.
The connection is "having placed [her] upon his own lap.
Here, the physical gesture (*abhinaya*) consists of placing her upon his chest,
while the verbal act (*vācika*) consists of coaxing or consoling her.

The term "this" (*imam*) refers by means of the word *idam* to the fawn-cub, which is the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*). Furthermore, there is the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) consisting of longing, manifested through parental affection (*vātsalya*).
For this longing is indeed indistinguishable from the love one feels for one's own son.
The connection between the distinctions of longing and passion is perceived;

however, the word "spṛhā" (longing) itself [expresses] love. Thus, this emotion consisting of passion (*rati*), which has affection (*vātsalya*) as its nature, is understood here through the four [categories], beginning with the ensuants (*anubhāva*).
This same [analysis] should be applied to other categories as well.
Regarding "possessing flavor" (*rasavat*): this [poem] possesses flavors such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, which have been clearly demonstrated.
It is the locus of its own words, the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas), the transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāvas), the determinants (vibhāvas), and the dramatic representations (abhinaya).
In dramatic performance, nine aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally recognized: the erotic, the comic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful.

These nine [rasas], beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), are, as appropriate, essentially the nourishment of the nine stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) such as love (rati), by virtue of being the means for attaining the four aims of human life (caturvarga) and the basis for avoiding their opposites.

Therefore, because they are to be tasted (āsvādya) in such a form, they are designated by the technical term *rasa*, which is based on a specific distinction of that tasting. However, in the case of [transitory emotions] such as despondency (nirveda), since there is an absence of such a thing to be tasted, the technical term *rasa*—which is based on a specific ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—does not apply.

However, with the intention of expressing merely the quality of being relishable (*āsvādyatva*), the application of the term *rasa* (flavor) to those [transitory emotions] is not contradictory, just as it is used for sweet, sour, and other tastes.

As it has been stated, following the enumeration of the *śṛṅgāra* and other [primary] *rasas*: “The teachers have declared that these [transitory emotions], like the sweet and others, possess the nature of *rasa* because they are tasted (*rasanāt*);
since that [quality of being tasted] exists fully even in *nirveda* and the rest, they too are *rasas*.”
Regarding this, they say:

"Since the two [types of characters] other than those belonging to the four aims of life (caturvarga) are to be attained and avoided respectively, such a rasa is considered to be one that is not to be tasted due to the differentiation of consciousness. Thus it is said.

The word "sa" (that) means a particularity of consciousness. By the phrase "of such a kind," it is stated that for a practitioner of the Tantras, the term *rasa* (taste/flavor) in relation to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments is based on a specific type of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*).
The comprehension of these nine rasas, beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), occurs through five means, such as their own words.
As stated by Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa: “Rasas have five forms.
Among these, "their own words" refers to the words "erotic" and so forth, which are the designators of the erotic and other rasas.

The nine stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and the rest, are known as the material causes (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*). The transitory emotions (*saṃcāribhāva*), however, such as despondency (*nirveda*) and the rest, take the form of specific states of those flavors.

The determinants (*vibhāva*), on the other hand, are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) of these [emotions], consisting of women and the like, as well as the seasons, garlands, ointments, and so forth.
The four types of acting, beginning with the physical (*āṅgika*), are the effects produced by the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).

When a poem clearly manifests the emergence of flavors such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) by serving as the locus for these five elements—beginning with the word itself—either collectively or individually, that poem is "possessing flavor" (*rasavat*).
Indeed, the flavors are its ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
An illustration of this:
As he was thus meditating upon all the virtues of Pārvatī,
Kandarpa, his resolve having been fully gathered, became powerful.
Even as his body perspired,
he bore a multitude of horripilations resembling a mass of filaments within the buds of *kadamba* flowers.
For a moment her face was adorned by a gaze pregnant with longing, for a moment motionless with anxiety, and for a moment languid with joy.
The "bud-calyx of the *kadamba*" refers to the interior of the *kadamba* bud;
herein is composed the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) characterized by the longing of separation (*abhilāṣika-vipralambha*) of the Blessed One.
Its direct expression is: "Kandarpa is powerful."
The permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) is manifested there by its own name as "Kandarpa.
For the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) consists essentially in the nourishment of *rati* (erotic passion),
and for young people, *rati* is of the nature of love (*manmatha*).
Therefore, because it expresses a particular kind of pleasure (*rati*), the word *kandarpa* here is the direct term for the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*).

Furthermore, the transitory emotions (*saṃcārin*)—longing, anxiety, and joy—are manifested by their own respective words. The two involuntary states (*sāttvika*), perspiration and horripilation, are also presented by their own words; moreover, these two also function as transitory emotions.
Because it is a specific state of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) for those of a sattvic nature, it functions as a transitory emotion (*saṃcārībhāva*), like despondency (*nirveda*) and others.
As for the determinants (*vibhāva*), they are indicated by the phrase "as he meditated thus" (*iti bhāvayatastasya*).
For the Blessed Lady, being contemplated as endowed with her various qualities, is the determinant (*vibhāva*).
In this context, the *abhinaya* (acting) specified is the acting of the side-glance (*apāṅga-abhinaya*), as indicated by the word "with a glance.
Therefore, here the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) of longing (*abhilāṣika*) is manifested through the five means, such as its own verbal expression.
In the same way, other sentiments (*rasas*) may also be illustrated.

Since *rasas* and *bhāvas* are the causes of the excellence of poetic beauty, it is not yet being investigated whether they constitute the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) of poetry or its very life (*jīvita*), for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Furthermore, the essential nature of *rasa* and *bhāva* has not been analyzed here, as it is not the immediate subject at hand and would require extensive discussion.
Ūrjasvin (the forceful):
The composition of emotions and sentiments that proceed from impropriety due to causes such as passion, anger, and so forth, is called ūrjasvin. (UKSS 4.5)

In some cases, indeed, the composition of sentiments (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*) is carried out in a manner that does not contradict the knowledge of the treatises (*śāstra*), while in other cases it is done in a manner that contradicts them.
Among these, where their composition is carried out in a manner that does not contradict the knowledge of the treatises, there the *preya* ornament and the *rasavat* ornament are said to exist.

However, where there is opposition to that [norm], and where there is opposition to worldly convention rooted therein—when the sentiments (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*) pertaining to such subjects are composed, that becomes the *ūrjasvin* (forceful) poetic figure.
For in that case, sentiments and emotional states caused by passion, hatred, and delusion are depicted through impropriety.
Precisely for this reason, because it possesses the force (*ūrjas*) or power of being constructed through one's own imagination, it receives the designation *ūrjasvin*.
In the expression "jyotsnātamisra," the word *urjasvin* [is applied] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.114.
An illustration of this is as follows:
"His desire grew in such a way that he proceeded to seize the daughter of the Snowy Mountain by force, having approached her while she was observing a vow of truth."

In this context, the forceful abduction of the Blessed One—who transcends all the world—by making her his wife while she was still a maiden, is contrary to the conventions of the scriptures and is composed as a cause for the intensification of passion;
by that, there is *ūrjasvitā* (vigor).
In that regard, the phrase "there Kāma increased" is the direct expression (*svaśabda*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Since it consists of the intensification of delight (*rati*) and thus has the nature of increasing desire (*kāma*), the word "desire" (*kāma*) is included within this [term *śṛṅgāra*].

Regarding that *rati* which constitutes the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of *śṛṅgāra*, the phrase "the daughter of the Snowy Mountain" (*himagireḥ sutām*) expresses its objective determinant (*ālambanavibhāva*). By the word "forcibly" (*haṭhena*), the transitory mental state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) characterized by agitation (*āvega*) is indicated.
The phrase "having abandoned the path of the righteous" is a vain effort;
rather, the gesture of "being intent on gathering [them]" is the indicative mark (*anubhāva*) belonging to the body.
Thus, in this context, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), characterized by its intensity, is indicated through these five elements, beginning with the explicit word.
In this way, *ūrjasvin* (the forceful) may also be illustrated in other cases of rasa and bhāva.
As for *paryāyokta* (periphrasis): "Paryāyokta is that which is expressed by means of another manner."
By means of that which is of the nature of comprehension, devoid of the functions of the signified and the signifier.
The function or operation of the signifier—that is, the expressive word—is the communication of the expressed meaning.

The function of the signified—that is, the expressed meaning—is its transition into a relation with another expressed meaning through the power of expectancy, proximity, and semantic fitness (*ākāṅkṣā-saṃnidhi-yogyatā*).
And even without such an operation of the signifier and the signified, there occurs—by way of another method—the nature of comprehension consisting in the capacity of the meaning itself.
That which is understood—even if not explicitly stated by its own name—is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), because it is apprehended through an indirect verbal operation.
By means of that [understood object], the meaning of the poem is adorned through its own internal connection.
An example of this is as follows:
By whom the wives of the elephant-demon were made to have hanging tresses, tearful eyes, breasts reddened by the blows of his hands, and their bracelets broken.
Even he whose body was scorched was thus agitated by that which was done;
homage be to that Makarakeṭu (the god of love) of irresistible prowess!

In this case, qualities such as having long locks of hair, being of the nature of effects, lead one to understand the slaughter of the demon Gajāsura, which serves as their cause—even though that slaughter is untouched by the operations of the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka).
And by that meaning, understood through such a striking mode of presentation (vicchitti), those meanings such as having long locks of hair are embellished.
Therefore, Paryāyokta is an ornament (alaṅkāra).

The Composed (*samāhita*) [state] is that which consists of the binding of tranquility arising from the occurrence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and their semblances (*tadābhāsa*); it is a form devoid of any other external stimuli (*anubhāva*). (UK 4.7)

In this context, it has been stated that aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*) are of two kinds: those that are not contrary to the conventions of the treatises and those that are contrary to them.
Among these, those flavors and emotional states that are not contrary to the conventions of the treatises are what is intended here by the term "flavors and emotional states."
However, those which are contrary to them are merely semblances (*tadābhāsa*) of them.

When the activity of these *rasas* and *bhāvas*, as well as their semblances—which consists in their connection with their own substrates—is brought to a state of cessation, the figure of speech *samāhita* (composed) occurs.
For in that case, the "composing" (*samādhi*) of those *rasas* and *bhāvas* constitutes their reconciliation (*parihāra*).
The word *samāhitam* (composed) is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

Now, one might object: "If the presence of *rasa* and so forth is excluded from that poetry, then, by the cessation of the previously mentioned *rasa* and other elements and the introduction of a different *rasa*, it would follow that the poetic figures such as *rasavat* and others have entered [into the definition]. Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "having a form devoid of other *anubhāvas*."
That which is described as such is a form that is entirely devoid of the manifestations (*anubhāva*) and so forth belonging to another rasa or similar aesthetic element.

In this state, because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the preceding rasas and so on have become firm, even when those [preceding rasas] have subsided, the essential nature of other rasas does not manifest; or, even if it were to manifest, it is obscured by something due to the exigencies of the dramatic action.
In that regard, there is the ornament of *samāhita* (concentration).
An example of it is as follows:
"Then, having seen his beloved's gaze and the playful movement of her eyebrows..."
The complexion of the face becomes serene, and it is filled with horripilation and perspiration.
Causing all his limbs to burn with the fever of passion,
Giriśa approached the Daughter of the Mountain with words of greeting.
"Composing himself" means establishing [his mind] in his own true nature;
because the term *samādadhat* is used here as a habitual form (*abhyasta*), the augment *num* does not apply.

In this context, the Blessed One has effected the concealment of those "consequents" (*anubhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), such as the longing glances toward his beloved, by means of the "state" (*bhāva*) consisting of composure (*avahittha*), which is characterized by the suppression of outward appearance.
As it was said— "preceded by *svasti*"—
by this, indeed, the concealment of the [original] form is demonstrated.
The *udātta* (elevated) [is as follows]:
A subject that is exalted and prosperous, as well as the conduct of great-souled beings,
serves as a means of illustration and does not constitute actual historical narrative.
*Ṛddhi* (prosperity) is the abundance of wealth such as gold and the like; an object endowed with that is *udātta* (lofty). And by means of that, the meaning of the poem is adorned.
An illustration of this is as follows:
"And he said that, because even the ornaments of the Śabara women were made of pearls from the Veṇu and Kuñjara elephants [in his belly]."
There, the Gandhamādana peak rises into the sky with its summits composed of emerald, sapphire, beryl, and ruby.
Its upper slopes consist of excellent golden lands,
and the great emerald Vindhya mountain rests at its base.
At the time of universal dissolution when the earth was sinking into the netherworld, his descent occurred along with it; yet his arrival remained unmanifested.
The connection is that she whose form is of such a kind is your daughter, Himārdrī.
*Kroḍa* means a boar;
*puṣṭya* refers to a particular kind of gem.
Gandhamādana is a particular mountain.
The foothills (*upatyakā*) are the regions of land situated at the base of the mountains.
The primary [type of] gold is *kārtasvara* and so forth.
Arvindhra is a mountain;
saṃkṣaya is the end of the eon (kalpānta).
Because the region adjacent to the earth has descended below the ground and thus becomes distinct from the earth, the extent of the Himalayas is revealed at the end of the eon (*kalpa*).
Herein, the accumulation of jewels and other treasures is fixed;
therefore, this is sublime (*udātta*).

And its status as an ornament [of poetry] arises from its suggesting a result—such as a jewel—that transcends the world. Thus, one type of *udātta* (the sublime) has been described based on a magnificent object. However, the *udātta* style does not consist solely of magnificent objects; it also includes the actions of those with vast aspirations who are intent upon the attainment of a goal or the avoidance of misfortune. As it has been said:
And regarding the phrase "the conduct of the great-souled ones":

when the activities of those with vast resolve are being described, it is not well-stated that there is an inclusion here of the *rasavat* ornament because of its being a cause for the apprehension of sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
This is because the activities of one with vast resolve function here as a subordinate sentence-meaning by way of indicating another primary subject matter.
Indeed, in this case, the conduct of a Great Being does not fall within the scope of the primary purport of the statement,
because the statement is intended to indicate another underlying meaning (*arthāntara*).

And where aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) are generally perceived, they constitute the "rasavat" ornament, because they serve as the locus of the sentence's repose and are experienced as the nourishment of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), which are the means for attaining or avoiding the four aims of human life and their opposites.
It occurs.
Therefore, how could there even be a scent of the *rasavat* ornament here?
As it has been said: "It has attained the status of being merely indicative; it has not become the actual plot (*itivṛtta*)."
An illustration of this is as follows:
"Though he remained motionless even when his broad shoulders were repeatedly rubbed by her firm breasts, a daughter was born to him, moist with snow."

Here, while the stability of the Himalayas constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), the activity of the Blessed One in his Boar incarnation—who was intent on uplifting the three worlds—serves as the cause for the apprehension of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). Because it functions as a subordinate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*), it becomes a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇībhūta*).
"Ādikroḍa" refers to the Primordial Boar (*Ādivarāha*).
In this same manner, examples may be cited where other sentiments (*rasa*) likewise function as secondary characteristics.

*Śliṣṭa* (Pun): A composition is called *śliṣṭa* here when words that are pronounced with a single effort and bear the same phonetic form appear distinct through differences in qualities such as the *svarita* accent. (UKSS 4.9)
Let that [poetry] be recognized as distinguished by the expression of both meaning and word, generating a flash of genius (*pratibhā*) through words that encompass other poetic ornaments.

In this regard, when there is a desire to express multiple meanings simultaneously for words that possess various senses, there are two possible courses of action. First, the established doctrine of Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa is that words are differentiated according to their distinct meanings.
Among those words differentiated by meaning, some can be employed by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application), while others cannot.
Those words whose consonants (*hal*), vowels (*svara*), places of articulation (*sthāna*), efforts (*prayatna*), and so forth are identical, can be employed by means of *tantra*.

However, where there is a distinction among consonants (*hal*) based on their being single or multiple, among vowels (*svara*) based on their being acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and so forth, among places of articulation (*sthāna*) based on their being labial, dental, bilabial, and so forth, and among efforts (*prayatna*) based on their being light (*laghu*) or heavy (*aguru*), it is impossible to apply them by the method of *tantra* (simultaneous or common application),
because *tantra* requires a common form.
As it has been said:
"The tantra would be common. This being the case, those [phonemes] which can be articulated by means of the tantra are to be articulated with a single effort.
In that case, there is a pun on the true meaning;
as it has been said:
"Of those [words] pronounced with a single effort."
Likewise, when words that bear the "shadow" or similarity of those very words uttered with a single effort are employed in composition, it is *śabda-śliṣṭa* (verbal punning).
This is because, when one word is being uttered, another word—though not actually uttered—is also present through the force of similarity.
As it has been said: "And [of those] bearing its very shadow."
"Śliṣṭa" (paranomasia) is a composition characterized by distinctions such as the *svarita* accent and other qualities;
thus, it should be understood as being distinguished by its verbal expression.
And this *śliṣṭa*, though of two kinds, attains the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) by way of generating the suggestion of ornaments such as simile (*upamā*).
Therefore, because it leaves no room for others within its own domain, it sets aside other figures of speech; for those [other figures] have scope in different domains.
As it has been said:
"Generating through words a flash of insight (*pratibhā*) that falls within other ornaments,
[in] two ways"— the meaning is that here there is merely the flash of insight regarding other ornaments, but not the actual composition of words (*padabandha*).
Thus, both the paronomasia based on sound (*śabda-śleṣa*) and the paronomasia based on meaning (*artha-śleṣa*) have been defined.
An example of them is as follows:
"And she herself shone with hands radiant like sprouts, copper-red..."
Like the morning twilight, she bestows the desired fruits upon those who long for them.
With a face like a moonstone, with hair as lustrous as great sapphire,
possessing the splendor of pearls, she is the jewel of the world of women, with feet like tender sprouts of ruby.
Even the report of the absence of the *apārijāta* tree brought the splendor of the *Nandana* grove to the earth;
though Abindusundarī remained forever without a drop [of sweat], she was constantly dripping with drops of loveliness.
The word "ca" (and) implies that not only are you the daughter of such a mountain as the Himālaya, but you yourself are also of such a nature.
In this regard, the Blessed Lady shines with her two hands— hands which are radiant and glowing, like tender sprouts, white and coppery-red.
The morning twilight, however, shines with the rays—meaning the beams—of the sun, Bhāskara, which are as pale-copper as young sprouts.

In both cases here, there is a similarity with the *halāhala* poison; therefore, because it is possible to pronounce [the word] by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application), this is a *śleṣa* based on meaning (*artha-śleṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "bestowing what is beneficial" (*hitapradā*) for those greedy for fruits that cannot be obtained through ease (*asvāpa*): in the context of the Goddess, the meaning is that she bestows the desired object upon those who are greedy for such fruits.

In the context of the morning twilight (*prabhātasandhyā*), however, the meaning is that she bestows unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—which is beneficial—for one who is not greedy for the fruit of sleep (*svāpa*), namely the cessation of fatigue, because he is engaged in the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*). Thus is her nature described.

And here, in the former position, because it is a single compound (*aikapadya*), there is an udātta accent on the final syllable according to the rule for *thā-thādi* compounds (Pāṇini 6.2.144). In the latter case, however, because *asvāpaphalalubdhe* and *hitapradā* are separate words, they possess different accents.
In the case of *asvāpaphalalubdha*, because the first member of the compound retains its original accent according to Pāṇini 6.2.2 (*tatpuruṣe tulyārtha...*), it is udātta on the initial syllable.
However, in the case of *hitaprada*, [the accentuation follows Pāṇini 6.2.140].
144) Just as [the word] *asvāpa* has its final vowel accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of its initial accent,

there is thus a difference in accent (*svarabheda*) here. Furthermore, in both cases— namely, in *asvāpa* for the vowel *a* and in *phalalubdhe* for the vowel *e*— there is also a difference in articulatory effort (*prayatnabheda*) due to the respective presence or absence of lightness (*lāghava*).
Therefore, it is impossible to pronounce them simultaneously.
However, when one word is uttered here, there is the comprehension of another word due to its similarity to it;
thus, this is a *śabdaśleṣa* (phonetic pun).
And both of these— meaning-pun (arthaśleṣa) and word-pun (śabdaśleṣa)— serve as the cause for the emergence of a simile (upamā).
Here, the dawn twilight is the standard of comparison (upamāna),
and the Blessed Lady is the object of comparison (upameya).

The word *iva* indicates the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). However, apart from the word itself, there exists no common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) here that resides in the referent (*artha*).
Therefore, this is not a simile (*upamā*), but rather a paronomasia (*śleṣa*) which serves as the cause for the emergence of a semblance of a simile (*upamāpratibhotpattihetu*).
Regarding the phrase *indukāntamukhī*: the Blessed Lady is such because her face is as beautiful as the moon;
likewise, she has glossy, long, black hair;
and she is such that she has abandoned (*muktā*) all lack of beauty (*aśrī*), meaning she is devoid of any ugliness.
And she is preeminent in the three worlds.

Likewise, she is one whose sprout-like feet possess a redness (*rāga*) like that of a lotus (*padma*), being of such a form. Furthermore, by means of a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on the arising of a visualized image, [she is described] as having the nature of a collection of rubies existing within the belly of the three worlds.
Then the subject at hand is perceived as having its form obscured by the splendor of moonstones, sapphires, pearls, and rubies;
because it possesses limbs composed of such jewels directly, it is understood as being of the nature of the abundance of gems contained within the belly of the three worlds.
And here, in the phrase "muktāśrīḥ," there is a variation in accent.
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent of the prior member [prevails]," the prior member retains its original accent;
whereas in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because of the rule regarding the final acute accent of a compound, the final syllable is accented.
However, among the remaining words, there is no difference in accent.
However, effort (*prayatna*), heaviness (*gurutva*), and lightness (*agurutva*) exist as objects of their respective phonemes, excluding the word *trijagadratna*.
Therefore, in those cases, there is verbal *śleṣa* (punning).
But for the word *trijagadratna*, since no distinction whatsoever exists in either case, it is a semantic *śleṣa*.

Regarding the phrase *apārijātavārtāpi*: because the Blessed One is "one whose enemies have not been born" (*ajātaśatru*), there is no news of a multitude of enemies; furthermore, his splendor captivates the minds of all. Thus, she is one whose glory is like that of the *nandana* grove.
Moreover, by virtue of being situated in the midst of water, she is as beautiful as the moon reflected in the waters, and her streams of loveliness flow perpetually.

But when this blessed lady, by means of a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) which serves as the basis for the arising of a metaphorical suggestion (*rūpakapratibhā*) because the word *nandanaśrī* denotes a different meaning characterized by the splendor of a celestial garden (*devodyāna*), attains this state, then— by virtue of relying upon that [metaphor] and through the consideration of words such as *apārijātavārtāpi*—
there occurs the manifestation of another *śleṣa* which is the cause for the appearance of a contradiction (*virodha*).
Indeed, the splendor of a celestial garden does not exist without the account of the specific tree known as the pārijāta;
nor does that tree stand upon the earth.

In the expression "abindusundarī," however, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) which serves as the cause for perceiving a contradiction: how could drops of loveliness (*lāvaṇyabindu*) flow forth from one whose beauty (*saundarya*) is not present in [ordinary] drops (*bindu*)?

In the case of *apārijātavārtāpi*, even here, since it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one from whom news of the enemy's birth has departed," the initial member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) according to the rule *prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*.
In the alternative view that it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would have an acute accent on the final syllable.

In the case of *abindusundarī*, because it is a simile meaning "beautiful like a water-drop" (*abinduvat sundarī*), the word *abindu* retains its original accent according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-*.
And because its first member ends in the locative case (saptamī), it is accented on the first syllable by this very rule as a *prakṛtisvara*.

In the case of *abindusundarī*, however, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), that same accent applies by virtue of the first member retaining its original accent (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
Therefore, there is no difference in accent between the two here.
However, due to the variety of the letter *ca* produced by a difference in effort, there is a verbal pun (*śabdaśleṣa*).
Thus ends the fourth section in the *Laghuvṛtti* on the *Udbhaṭālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha*, composed by the illustrious Pratīhāra Indurāja.
Now begins the fifth section:
Apahnuti (Concealment), Viśeṣokti (Peculiar Allegation), Virodha (Contradiction), and Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing).
And Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description), Vyājastuti (Artful Praise), and Vidarśanā (Illustration).

Furthermore, others have declared these ornaments of speech to be: the comparison of the compared with the comparer (upameyopamā), joint description (sahokti), commixture (saṃkara), and exchange (parivṛtti).
Apahnuti (Concealment):
Apahnuti is also desired when there is a suggestion of something internal;
it is composed by the wise through the denial of a real fact.

Where the actual, existing object characterized as the *upameya* (the thing compared) is denied, and through the superimposition of the form of the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison), the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* [is established]— this is the figure of speech *Apahnuti*.
And here, regarding the existing contextual object, it is said that although it exists, the relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* shines forth in an indistinct form.
"Something with an internal comparison" (*kiñcidantargatopamā*): an example of this is as follows— "This is indeed not austerity; this is the deadly *hālāhala* poison."
Especially for those like you, who are as tender as the crescent moon.
Here, by concealing the true nature of the penance under discussion and superimposing upon it the form of a particular *hālāhala* poison, its similarity to that poison is made known.
And because the object of comparison (the penance) has been concealed here, this similarity to *hālāhala* poison is not manifest in its explicit form.
*Hālāhala* is a specific type of poison that kills instantaneously.
Poetic Peculiarization (viśeṣokti):

When there is a connection to the non-production of an effect despite the presence of the full collection of causal powers, that which is intended for the sake of expressing a particularity is called poetic peculiarization. (UK 5.4)

Even when there is a complete assembly of causal factors (*kāraka*) possessing their respective potencies (*śakti*), that connection to the non-arising of the fruit of an action—which serves to make known some specific qualification—is *viśeṣokti* (the description of a specific).
And it has two varieties.
In one case, even though the collection of causes is present, the effect does not arise; regarding that non-arising, the cause [for its non-production] is explicitly stated by the author himself.
In some cases, however, it is understood through the power of the meaning; as he says:
"By means of an indicated cause and by the non-perception of a cause, its charmingly subtle bondage is seen in two ways within the object of observation. (UK 5.5)
Non-perception is non-apprehension.
An example of the second type of division is as follows:
birth in a family of great prosperity, beauty, a friend who remembers [one], and youth.
Nevertheless, no one attains happiness, nor is their intellect amazed.

In this instance, although the complete causes for the attainment of happiness— namely, the accumulation of wealth, physical beauty, and youth— are present, the non-arising of that attainment of happiness which is the fruit of action is described in order to demonstrate the specific excellence of the previously mentioned causes of happiness through the figure of speech known as *vismaya-vibhāvanā* (the manifestation of wonder).
Furthermore, the cause [for this non-attainment] is understood here by the force of the context, even though it is not explicitly stated by the author himself.

In this context, the word *vidhivaidhuryādi* (deficiency of fate, etc. is employed with the intention of denoting excellence of form, because "form" (*rūpa*) is invariably concomitant with the physical body.
"Smarasuhṛd" refers to youth;
for it is in youth that one becomes oriented toward the God of Love (*manmatha*).
An example of the first variety [of *parivṛtti*] is as follows:
"Having seen your conduct thus so disordered, not even a single word arises from me to ask anything, even though I am in a hurry. (Udbhaṭa, Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṃgraha 5.3)
Here, although the causes characterized by the haste of inquiry are present, the non-occurrence of the speech of inquiry is described;
and through that, a specific quality of the cause of the inquiry, known as "the manifestation of wonder," is understood.
Furthermore, the cause in this case—the sight of the Blessed Lady’s faltering movements—is explicitly stated by the author himself.

Contradiction (virodha)—the statement of an action contrary to either a quality or an action for the purpose of expressing a specific distinction; that they call contradiction. (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra 5.6)

Where a poet, by means of a word— whether it be a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*kriyā*), or a substance (*dravya*)— or by the employment of the particle *vā* (or), expresses through speech born of his own creative intuition (*pratibhā*) another object that is contrary to it, whether of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*), for the purpose of conveying some particular distinction, that is the figure of speech called *virodha* (contradiction).
In the course of explaining the definitions of the poetic figures (alaṅkāras) based on qualities (guṇa), actions (kriyā), and substances (dravya), their essential natures were stated.
Action (kriyā) is the cause of production; speech in which that [action] is predominant is "speech concerning action" (kriyāvacaḥ).

Indeed, through the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of the poet, fresh objects of expression are fashioned that are entirely distinct from the dry and harsh objects created by the ancient Prajāpatis; they are full of aesthetic flavor (*saras*).
Therefore, it is said that [the word] "expressive of action" (*kriyāvac*) [is used]. An example of this is as follows:
Or rather, what can I do? This astonishment makes me speechless: where is this appearance of yours, and where is this proficiency in asceticism?

Here, the objection to what was previously introduced by the statement "my words do not arise" is made by the phrase "yadveti. Alternatively, the connection is as follows: "What can I do? Being rendered speechless by wonder, I say: 'Where [is this] of yours?
This very wonder makes me speak."

In whose mind does the hardness of the jasmine, the crescent moon, and the plantain not appear when one beholds the softness of your limbs?
The meaning is: in whose mind, upon seeing the delicacy of your body, would the hardness of *mālatī* flowers and the like not appear?
Here, a similarity characterized by hardness is established between non-contextual objects such as *mālatī* flowers and others.
The word "draṣṭuḥ" (of the beholder) is formed with the suffix *tṛn*.
And in the phrase "the softness of your limbs" (*tvadaṅgamārdavam*), there is a prohibition of the genitive case according to the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā-* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).
An example of the second type [of the genitive used with a word ending in a kṛt suffix] is: "the yoga-band, the mass of matted hair, the bark garment, and the deer-skin."
If these [ornaments] are suitable for your body, then let it be said.
Here, a common attribute—namely, the fitness for contact with the body of the Blessed Lady—is established even for the yogapaṭṭa and other items relevant to the context.
*Tāravītvak* means bark;
*aṅgasya* means of the body.
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Praise):
"That praise of another subject which is irrelevant to the present context, yet is connected to the matter at hand, is Aprastutapraśaṃsā. (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra 5.8)

Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) is the composition of another subject that has departed from the immediate context— the topic under discussion— due to the lapse of the occasion for its description.
Nor does it follow that this figure is like the incoherent ravings of a madman, because it connects the subject at hand with some quality of its own.
As it has been said: "That which is connected to the subject at hand.
An example of this is as follows:
"Those who have not yet attained enjoyment [of their fruits] undergo old age within their own bodies."
Even the splendors of forests in difficult regions possess an abundance of fruits and flowers.

In this context, the beauty of the forests situated in that region where it is possible to travel only with great difficulty is described as being extraneous [to the subject], by virtue of the exhaustion of one’s own body.
Through these [descriptions], the activity of the Goddess—which serves as the object of comparison—is understood to possess such a form by way of similarity based on her own inherent nature.
The word *durgā* is formed with the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule *suduro’dhikaraṇe*.
Circumlocutory Praise (vyājastuti): Where, by the very nature of the power of words,
what appears to be censure is actually intended as praise, that is considered circumlocutory praise.

In this context, the censure is understood as if it were conveyed by that inherent nature of the expressive power of words—their eagerness to convey meaning—which consists in being restricted to a specific object; yet it is not censure itself, because when praise arises from the capacity for reflecting upon the word-meanings and becomes the primary sense of the sentence, it functions as a subordinate sentence-meaning.
For this very reason, he says:
In reality, however, praise is intended [as censure].
"In reality" means by the force of the context.
In that case, there occurs the poetic figure known as *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
For that is praise under the guise of censure;
therefore, it is "Praise by Guise" (vyājastuti). An example of it is as follows:
Fie upon this peerless perfection of your beauty,
since even in the three worlds no suitable husband can be found for you!

In this context, that impairment of the excellence of her form caused by the expression of reproach, which is directly touched upon by the operation of the words, does not terminate in itself; for it terminates in the demonstration of the extraordinary excellence of the Blessed Lady’s form, which arises through the power of the sense.
Therefore, it constitutes the meaning of a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākyārtha*).
Therefore, this is *vyājastuti* (feigned praise),
because the excellence of her form is being praised under the guise of censure. In the phrase "dhig ananyopamām," the accusative case is used according to the rule "ubhasarvatasoḥ kārye."
Illustration (vidarśanā)—

where one imagines a relationship between things that do not exist or that do exist, such that there is the state of being the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, that is called illustration. (UK 5.10)

Where the relation between things, being inherently untenable, results in the state of being the object of comparison and the subject of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*), or where it establishes itself through the conceptualization of that very state of comparison,
there is *vidarśanā*, because of the presentation of a distinguished meaning consisting of that state of comparison and contrast.
An illustration of that [type of incongruity] is as follows:
"Even though she is beautiful, a loving woman, when deprived of a husband suited to her, bears a lack of splendor like a moonless night. (UKss 5.9)
Vidhu is the moon;
vibhāvarī is the night.

Here, this state of being the object (karmatva) belonging to the lack of splendor of the night when it is devoid of the moon does not find its logical connection (samanvaya) with the act of nourishing performed by the woman in love.
For one person does not bear the splendor belonging to another;
therefore, the syntactic connection of the word-meanings here is untenable.
However, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is the point where the meaning of the sentence comes to rest: "He bears a splendor like that of the night of Kṛṣṇa."

Thus it is: this is an example where the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is conceived despite a lack of actual connection between the things.

However, an example of that variety of *vidarśanā* (illustration) wherein the [poet] establishes his own position by conceiving the relationship between the standard and object of comparison through the congruence of word-meanings (*padārtha-samanvaya*) is not seen in Udbhaṭa’s manuscript.
But this is the example given for it by Bhāmaha:

"This sun, its radiance dimmed, desires to go toward the setting; it announces to men that the rising is for the sake of falling. Thus, in that context, this inclination of the sun toward setting—which is devoid of the splendor expanding at the time of its first rising—[is described].

For the illustrious one endowed with that [insight], in relation to the causal agents (prayojyakartṛ), there is established a causative agency (*hetukartṛtva*) characterized by the performance of actions capable of bringing about an awakening whose result is the emergence and conclusion of [all things] through falling.
Indeed, seeing the radiant one in such a state, the illustrious ones perceive that for everything, as for the sun, there is an emergence ending in a fall.
And perceiving them to understand [the matter] in that way, he employs them by demonstrating his own condition, [saying]: "Just as this rise of mine ends in a fall, so too it is for you.

And since there is no sense of commanding or entreating here, the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is characterized solely by performing what is conducive to that [result], as in the examples: "The cow-dung (*kārīṣa*) causes one to study" or "Alms (*bhikṣā*) cause one to dwell.

By means of that relationship between the instigated and the instigator, a relationship of analogy and the object of analogy is implied: "O illustrious ones, just as this rise of mine leads to a fall, so too it will for you."

"Awake!"—by this connection of word-meanings, characterized by the relationship between the instigator and the instigated, there is an implied suggestion (ākṣepa) of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared for the purpose of establishing one's own self; thus, this is the second variety of *vidarśanā*.

*Saṃkara* (commingling)—and that is of four kinds, distinguished as: commingling of doubt (*saṃdeha*), commingling of word and meaning (*śabdārtha-vartin*), commingling of figures of speech expressed by a single word (*eka-śabdābhidhāna*), and commingling of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhaka*).
Among these, first, commingling of doubt (*saṃdeha-saṃkara*)—:
When multiple figures of speech are suggested simultaneously, yet it is impossible for them to function together,
and when there is no logical reason or fault to prefer one over the other, that is *saṃkara* (commixture).
When multiple figures of speech (alaṅkāra) are delineated and ascend into the mind, there occurs a confusion of doubt (saṃdehasaṃkara);
however, even in cases such as the confusion of expression by a single word (ekaśabdābhidhānasaṃkara), the delineation of multiple figures of speech is not possible.
For example:
Surely the edge of the discus, emerging from Murāri— the adversary of Naraka—
will fall upon your head like the Gaṅgā.

For here, the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared, as well as the cause of its manifestation— namely, *śleṣa* (punning)— is delineated as multiple ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).
Regarding the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared, the Ganges is first the standard of comparison.
The edge of the discus is the object of comparison;
"having emerged from Murāri" is the common attribute;
and here, the pun (śleṣa) finds its basis in the word *narakapratipanthin*.
For in one case it is the Dānava named Naraka, while in the other it is the Avīci hell and so forth;
and these two ornaments both enter into the single word "iva" (like/as if).

For neither the relation of standard of comparison and object compared, nor the *śleṣa* (punning) which causes its manifestation, acquires its own form without the word "like" (*iva*) and so forth in the absence of a compound. Therefore, two figures of speech have entered into a single expressive word, as in the case of the word "like. And if it were the case that a "doubtful commixture" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) occurs when there is the manifestation of multiple figures of speech, then one might suspect that in such instances as this, since the manifestation of multiple figures is possible, the consequence would be a doubtful commixture; anticipating this, it is said: "That [is] equal, because of the impossibility of their co-occurrence."
Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that it is impossible for multiple figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) to function—that is, to operate—simultaneously (*samaṃ yugapat*) in a manner consisting of the ornamenting of the object to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya-alaṅkaraṇātman*).

However, in the previously cited example, because the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is expressed by the word "emerged from the mouth of Murāri" (*murārinirgatā*), and because the word "obstacle to hell" (*narakapratipanthinī*) indicates the presence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is no impossibility of the simultaneous occurrence of multiple figures of speech.
Therefore, there is no confusion regarding doubt in that case.
Now, if it is argued that "doubt-confusion" (saṃdehasaṃkara) occurs when multiple figures of speech are suggested simultaneously and their coexistence is impossible,
then in a case where several figures are being suggested by mere intuition, that one for which there is supporting evidence (*pramāṇa*) should be accepted.
However, that for which there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is abandoned.

In this regard, since both the depiction of multiple ornaments (*anekālaṅkārollekha*) and the impossibility of their simultaneous occurrence (*tadvṛttyasaṃbhava*) are possible, one might suspect that the fault of "confusion through doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) would follow; anticipating this, it was stated: "and when there is no reason or flaw in favor of accepting one [of the two]."
*Nyāya* is the corroborating proof (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*);
*doṣa* is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Where there is a depiction of multiple figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) simultaneously, yet it is impossible for them to function together, and where neither a corroborating nor a subverting proof exists—whether collectively or individually—for the apprehension of one over the other, there is "blending through doubt" (*saṃdeha-saṃkara*).
Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence.

For instance: where both a proving and a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist in their entirety, one accepts that for which there is a proving means of valid cognition and rejects that which is accompanied by a subverting means of valid cognition; thus, the acceptance of one occurs.

Even where there is a presence of either a probative or a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to their mutual exclusion, in that case as well, one [of the two] is apprehended: because from among the various figures of speech being suggested by the *pratibhā*, that which is supported by a probative means of valid cognition is adopted; because that which is devoid of such a means of valid cognition is likewise abandoned; and because the other, which was previously suggested, is excluded by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). However, where there is an absence of both a probative and a subverting means of valid cognition, there is only doubt.
Thus, this confusion of doubt has been characterized. An example of it is as follows:
"Even though a bridegroom entirely worthy of you cannot be found,"
Nevertheless, I say this: let some respect be shown toward a human being somewhere.

Here, in the expression "the excellent moon" (*varendu*), there is the mention of two figures of speech: the compound metaphor (*rūpaka-samāsa-upamā*) in the sense of "the excellent one is indeed the moon," and the simile (*upamā*) in the sense of "the excellent one is like the moon.
And yet, the simultaneous occurrence of those multiple figures of speech is not possible.

Because a poetic figure achieves its purpose through the employment of only one figure, there is no application of probative or subversive evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here for the sake of selecting one from between two. For a probative means of knowledge, being present, would indicate the poetic figure by way of affirmation;

likewise, a subversive means of knowledge, by way of negating the poetic figure that is to be abandoned, establishes the previously mentioned acceptable figure as the one to be adopted through the method of remainder (*pāriśeṣya*).
In this case, however, because there is an absence of both a proving and a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is doubt;
therefore, it is the figure of speech *saṃkara* (commixture).
As for the figures of speech residing in word and meaning—
The figure of speech residing in both word and meaning occurs where figures of speech residing in words and those residing in meanings appear together in a single sentence;

that is, where figures of speech belonging to the word and figures of speech belonging to the meaning enter into a combination within one sentence, it is the "figure of speech of both word and meaning" (śabdārthālaṅkāra).
An example of this is as follows:
"If such is your resolve for the sake of a boon, do not make your petitioning in vain;
for every young man is bound at the feet by your beauty and is indeed your servant."
"Seeking a boon" means seeking a husband;
"servant" means a slave.
Here, there is a verbal ornament (śabdālaṅkāra) consisting of alliteration (anuprāsa), constructed with the letter *tha*.
There exists the figure of speech *arthālaṅkāra* known as *arthāntaranyāsa*.

To explain: here, the statement "Do not make your supplication in vain" implies that it is impossible not to make a request for an object one desires to obtain; since this [seeming impossibility] is presented, it is considered incongruous, and thus, in order to justify it, it is said: "For every youth, bound by your beauty, is indeed your servant."
One who possesses excellence of qualities does not seek [something],
but rather is sought after, as in the case of jewels and the like;
and you, by virtue of your beauty, possess such excellence of qualities.
Therefore, your desire for the object you wish to acquire is improper;
thus, this is a commingling of figures of speech residing in both the word and the meaning.
However, the confusion of denotation by a single word is said to occur because of the entry [of multiple meanings] into a single constituent part of a sentence.
When multiple figures of speech enter into a single portion of a sentence—that is, a part of a sentence—it is the *saṃkara* (commingling) known as "denotation by a single word.
An example of this is:
"Do not remain thus; you possess a beautiful *karṇikā* (pericarp/ear-ornament) with a fine luster and color."
A lotus pond depicted in a painting provides pleasure merely by being seen.

Here, there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), and the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) which serves as the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of that simile; these two figures of speech both enter into a single constituent of the sentence, namely the word *iva*.
For instance: *ambhojinī* is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and *gaurī* is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
The common property (*sādhāraṇo dharma*) is the quality of bestowing pleasure merely upon being seen; this constitutes a simile (*upamā*).

Furthermore, the phrase "a beautiful pericarp with a fine-colored coating" (*sacchāyavarṇikā cārukarṇikā*) is a pun (*śleṣa*), for while the colors (*varṇāḥ*) in a lotus-bed refer to pigments such as *rājavarta* and the like, in the case of Gaurī they refer to her fair complexion (*gauratvam*).
In the case of *ambhojinī*, *karṇikā* refers to the seed-vessel containing the honey of the lotus;
however, in the case of *gaurī*, it refers to beautiful ears.
Here, the suffix *kap* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*).
Therefore, this is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
And these two figures of speech have entered into a single constituent of the sentence, namely the word *iva*.
Consequently, this is a *saṃkara* (commixture) based on expression by a single word (*ekaśabdābhidhāna*).
As for the confusion between the embellished and the embellisher:
"Where figures of speech exist through mutual assistance, yet do not attain their own existence independently—that too is confusion (saṃkara). (UK 5.13)
Where there is a mutual relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between two things, that is *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile),
because the standard of comparison is compared by means of the object of comparison.
Now, is it not the case that the *upameya* is that which is contextual and connected to the expression of similarity?
The comparison is irrelevant to the context.

If, moreover, the status of the object of comparison (*upameya*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) were asserted here, then its contextual relevance (*prākaraṇikatva*) would be contradicted; anticipating this objection, it is said: "it leads to the abandonment of the alternative position."

The intention here is not to establish a relationship of similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison; rather, it is that these two alone exist in such a manner, and no other entity exists that is similar to them.
Therefore, since the intended meaning is the exclusion of any alternative position apart from these two positions, there is no mutual relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison.

It does not incur fault because, when its alternative position is abandoned during the process of deliberation, it remains as the meaning of an intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākyārtha*), just like the statement: "It is better to eat poison than to eat in the house of such a person.
For in this case, the eating of poison is certainly not being enjoined.
Because there is an intent to avoid eating in the house of a wicked person;
likewise here, because there is an intent to abandon other positions regarding the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
An example of this is as follows:
Just as the hunter Smara was not rejected by Hara, so too this [Smara], though unacknowledged by you, does not leave your body even for a moment, as if out of audacity.

In this context, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that "he does not abandon his audacity" acquires its true form through the power of a pun (*śleṣa*) which serves as the cause for the emergence of a simile (*upamā*): "By you, the hunter Smara was rendered bodiless (*anaṅga*), even though he was not [physically] rejected (*anaṅgīkṛta*).
For "rendered bodiless" (*anaṅga*) means made to be without a body (*aśarīra*), and "not rejected" (*anaṅgīkṛta*) means not refused (*anūrīkṛta*).
And since one who is not refused does not leave even for a moment, it is possible to fancy that his audacity is the cause [of his persistence].
By virtue of thatśleṣa (paronomasia), a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) has here acquired its own nature;
therefore, this is a commingling (saṃkara) of the "benefited" and the "benefactor.

Thus, this fourfold commingling has been described by relying on the various arrangements of alternatives, conjunctions, and the relationship of subordinate and principal among different figures of speech.
In that case, due to the conceptualization of multiple ornaments, there is a "confusion through doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*).

When two ornaments, residing respectively in the word and the meaning, exist with distinct substrata, there is a "confusion based on a fixed foundation" (*vyavasthāsamāśraya*) consisting of the ornaments residing in the word and the meaning.

However, in the case of confusion through expression by a single word, several ornaments enter into a single portion of a sentence simultaneously, such as at the beginning, by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

When there is a confusion between the object to be favored (anugrāhya) and the favorer (anugrāhaka), however, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) between two figures of speech.

Therefore, these four varieties of *saṃkara* (commixture) are based upon option (*vikalpa*), restriction (*vyavasthā*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), and the relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
[The fifth variety is] *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile)...
Where there is a mutual relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison,
they call that *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), which serves to exclude other alternatives.

Where there is a mutual relationship of standard of comparison (upamāna) and object of comparison (upameya) between two things, that is *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), because the standard of comparison is compared by means of the object of comparison. Now, it may be objected: the object of comparison is that which belongs to the context and is connected with the expression of similarity, while the standard of comparison is that which does not belong to the context.

If it were argued here that the status of the object of comparison (upameya) is being predicated of the standard of comparison (upamāna), then its contextual relevance (*prākaraṇikatva*) would be contradicted; anticipating this objection, it is stated: "leading to the abandonment of the alternative position" (*pakṣāntarahānigāmi*).

Here, the intent is not on the relationship between the standard and the object of comparison, but rather that these two alone exist in such a manner, and there exists no other distinct entity similar to them.

Therefore, since what is intended here is the exclusion of any alternative position apart from these two positions, the mutual relationship of standard and object of comparison does not incur any fault.

Since the exclusion of the alternative position is what is to be established, it stands as the meaning of the intermediate sentence—just like the saying, "It is better to eat poison than to eat in this man's house.
For here, the eating of poison is not actually enjoined, because the intent is the avoidance of eating in the house of a wicked person.
Likewise, in this case as well, the relationship of simile (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is not intended to be expressed, because the intent lies in the exclusion of the alternative position.
In battle, his discus—which resembles his hand—swiftly hurls the heads of his enemies like lotuses; and his hand, which resembles a wheel, wields that very discus.

In this context, since the word "yasya" (of whom) has been employed, the requirement for syntactic connection will be satisfied by the concordance of the pronoun "saḥ" (he) with that [relative clause] in the phrase "so 'pi vaikuṇṭhaḥ" (even he is Vaikuṇṭha). Furthermore, in the subsequent verses as well, the meaning of the relative pronoun "yat" must be rendered free of expectancy by that very same [correlative].
Here, there exists a mutual relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison between the hand and the discus.
And here the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is the cutting off of the enemy’s head with extreme swiftness.
This relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) culminates in the absence of any other standard of comparison;
for, at most, there could only be a mutual relationship of standard and object between these two, since there is no other standard of comparison for them.
Co-expression (sahokti): When two actions occurring at the same time and resting upon two distinct objects are expressed by a single word, that is considered co-expression by the wise. (UK 5.15)

Where two actions inherent in two objects are expressed by a single word through the principle of *tantra-vṛtti* (simultaneous application), there occurs the figure of speech called *sahokti* (conjoint narration).

Now, one might object: "In examples such as 'The autumn season withdrew [the lotuses] and [the clouds] gathered,' two actions inherent in two objects are likewise expressed by a single word; therefore, shouldn't the figure of *sahokti* apply there as well? Anticipating this objection, it is stated: "occurring at the same time."
Where two actions, each residing in two distinct entities, are expressed after understanding their simultaneity through a word such as *saha* (together), there exists the figure of speech *sahokti*.
Since this is not the case with *dīpaka*, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
And when simultaneity is illuminated by a word such as *saha*, there are two possible ways of understanding it.
Indeed, when two actions occur at the same time, those two actions are expressed as resting within their own respective substrates due to their equal status,

as in the case of "Devadatta and Yajñadatta eat together. However, when an action is expressed as resting in a single substrate, the connection of the other substrate with that action is understood through the power of reflecting upon the meaning of the word "together" (*saha*).
For example, as in the case of "Devadatta eats together with Yajñadatta.
Here, the second type of relation is resorted to;

for while the connection with the action is perceived in one instance through its verbal form, in the other it is inferred through its implied meaning, owing to the presence of an oblique mode of expression (*vakrabhaṇiti*).
